utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there are two documents to be exhibited from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I think we do. And I believe that one of them is the short part of interview with this witness made as preparation for, but not as part of, The Death of Yugoslavia film, and that's one matter which ought to be exhibited, with your leave. It's the passage, just to remind everybody, a translation difficulty over national/nationalistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the court deputy give that a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 878.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the other document, I think, that Your Honours may have had in mind as not yet having been produced was a document that had three excerpts we looked at from the accused's book -- the witness's book, Politics as a Conscientious Challenge, which contained entries, to remind you, the entries, "Bosnia is undoubtedly Serbian, and if any fundamentalists don't like it, they must pack their suitcases and leave." That's that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Politics as a Conscientious Challenge was admitted already. It is 876. I think it is Horvat's Ustasha Phantasmagorias.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, Your Honours, that one, indeed, hasn't yet been admitted and I've still got further questions to ask about it, because we've only looked at one excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And we have to keep abreast of the documents' exhibition. We don't want them to pile up. Now, Mr. Seselj, yesterday you commented that the cross-examiner was rude, or something to that effect. I want to make it clear to you that cross-examination can be vigorous and aggressive, and there is absolutely nothing wrong with that, and that it in no way absolves you of the responsibility to be courteous in your replies. It's not rudeness. Vigorous and aggressive cross-examination is not the same thing as being rude. The cross-examiner has a right to put his case to the witness of the other party. Mr. Nice, please start.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't reply. Mr. Nice, continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yesterday we were looking at extracts from Horvat's Ustasha Phantasmagorias, and, Mr. Seselj, if you'd be good enough, please, to go to the third of the three marked passages, which on the English is page 15 of 16, and in your version, Mr. Seselj, is the last sheet. We come to a passage within an overall heading "Serbs to Rally in Kumanovo Soon" but the highlighted passage, which of course you can always refer to the setting if necessary, reads as follows. And if Mr. Nort would place the English on the overhead projector, page 15 of 16. Don't worry if you haven't got it, I'll just read it out: "All those with an unclear conscience should fear us Serbs. They have reason to fear us. Us Serbs have forgotten and forgiven too much in history. We have told the Croats: Should they ever again resort to genocidal activities against the Serbian people, not only shall we take revenge for every victim but we shall also settle scores for the victims from World War I and World War II. However, we have not threatened them yet. We have not attacked a single Croatian village. We have only defended the Serbian villages. If we are not present in some villages or we are unable to defend them, we shall take revenge wherever the Croats are the weakest. We speak the language of force, the language of power, because the Serbian people are strong and powerful only when Serbia is united, when the Serbs are united." First of all, are these your words?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are my words from a text within the framework of a collection of works published under the title of "Horvat's Ustasha Phantasmagorias." The main text in the book is the text about Branko Horvat himself with respect to his book about Kosovo, and I say that from Ustasha positions he asked that Kosovo secede from Serbia and become a separate federal unit, or rather, republic. This is just one of those articles or texts and these are the words from that text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but these were views you expressed; is that right? And are they views which you still hold?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the views and positions that I will adhere to to the end of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when do you believe this text was first published? It may be a little difficult from the book to identify the first publication date. You may be able to help us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says it there for you, but you're not reading. Here we have the title of the text, the pre-electoral speech in Rakovica on the 4th of June, 1991. It says so there, above the text itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've been looking at it in the original. We've been looking at it in the translated passage. Very well. So in 1991, you thought it a responsible thing, did you, to say that you would take revenge --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- in respect to the victims of World War I and World War II, on people who hadn't presumably even been born until after the Second World War. Can you justify an educated person making such statements at a time of political difficulty?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is in your interpretation of it. Your interpretation is highly malicious. I am threatening here and saying: If the Croats dare and go ahead and engage in genocide activities against the Serbs, so I'm warning them, I'm cautioning them. So I am issuing the threat within a caution. This is the conditional again. And previously, on several occasions, I said, and you quoted one of my quotations, that I said that states and nations are punished for their crimes by loss of territory. We spoke about this yesterday, discussed it yesterday. So all my texts are a continuum. They follow on from one another. They are the development of one idea in detail, one detail after another. But you have to view everything within that context. So what is the purpose of this speech? It is a warning: Don't engage in genocide again. I did not say we will take revenge on individual Croats - that's not what I said - who were born after the war, but Croats as such, per se, Croats as a category.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... settling scores for the victims of World War I and World War II? Well, how are you going to settle those scores unless you settle them against those born after the Second World War, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is lacking there for you. A higher intelligence coefficient, Mr. Nice, IQ. I said how we were going to settle accounts; settle for war damage, the killing of civilians, looting and pilfering in Serbia during World War I, and that is highly documented. Then to settle accounts as far as World War II is concerned, the killing of a million Serbs under the Ustasha Croatian regime. And how are we going to take our revenge? By bringing Croatia down to three counties; Varazdin, Zagreb and Krizevac, which is, in fact, the true Croatia. All the rest was seized from the Serbian people along with the Vatican policy and turning the Serb Catholics into Croats. So that should be quite clear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so when we just look - and this is the last question I'll ask you about this passage - when we look at the last sentence and a half: "... we shall take revenge wherever the Croats are the weakest. We speak the language of force, the language of power, because the Serbian people are strong and powerful only when Serbia is united." That sentence and a half shouldn't have put any post-World War II occupants of Croatia in physical fear; is that right? It should just have exposed them to some anxiety about peaceful reoccupation of territory they improperly called Croatia. Is that what you're suggesting, something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, as far as peaceful, you can't ascribe that to me. I'm not particularly peaceful. I am in principle in favour of peace, but not at all costs, at all price, not at the price of Serb national interests and jeopardising those. And I never expressly spoke of peaceful policies. You can disqualify me for not being a peaceful man to your own taste, however, here what I'm saying is this: That we Serbs are powerful when we are united, and I am appealing for the highest possible degree of national unity among the Serbs, and I am fully conscious of the fact that the Croats would not even dare to secede and enter into a conflict with the Serbs had they not had powerful support from abroad. And every time when the Croats had an onslaught against the Serbs and engaged in genocidal activities, they had support, whether it be Austro-Hungary or Hitler's support. In this case, it was the Vatican's support and the support of all the Western powers. But countless times, in various speeches of mine and in this book, indeed, and in what you showed us yesterday, which was a speech --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you have responded to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What's significant for this trial is this, and I'll deal with it in two parts. First of all, my suggestion to you is that you were a dangerous and wicked man, generating anxiety on the parts of Serbs and generating the circumstances for violence. That's my allegation generally against you. The second part is that the accused did nothing to stop your -- or discourage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him deal with the first suggestion that you are putting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Dangerous and a wicked man, generating anxiety on the parts of Serbs and generating the circumstances for violence. That's what you were about.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whereas I think, Mr. Nice, that you are an underhand person, the most underhand person in the Hague Tribunal, and perfidious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have explained to you, Mr. Seselj, that the cross-examiner can be very strong, he can be vigorous, he can be aggressive in putting questions to you, and questions about your character. You're a witness for the accused, for the other party. And he's entitled to put his case to you. His case is that you're a dangerous person. That doesn't mean that he's perfidious. You are not allowed, by the Rules of this Court, to suggest that the Prosecutor is perfidious. You may say that about one of his witnesses, but not about him personally. So let us get that very, very clear. I will not allow you to make allegations about the character of the Prosecutor. That's not allowed in the system that we operate here. You perhaps come from a system where you're not accustomed to vigorous cross-examination. There is absolutely nothing wrong in what the Prosecutor has put to you. That is his case. And you must respond to it without suggesting matters which, in your view, reflect adversely on his character. And I will absolutely insist on that. So let us have an answer to the allegation that you're a dangerous person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Nice said that I was a dangerous person and wicked and vicious, and he is an underhand and perfidious man and he can't be rude to me and insult me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have cut you off there. If you continue like that, it will not be for the benefit of the accused, and you are here appearing on his behalf. When Mr. Nice says you're dangerous, he is putting his case to you. That is the Prosecution's case. It is not personal. It is his own assessment of what his case is on the evidence. And you must reply to it without making allegations about the Prosecution. That is the system which we operate here. That's how the adversarial system operates. So let us have an answer to the allegation that you're a dangerous person and that generally your conduct generated circumstances for violence. Is that true or is that not true? What is your response to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My response to that is this: Mr. Nice is a perfidious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not getting -- I've stopped. I've stopped you. I've explained to you that you're obliged to reply without suggesting that Mr. Nice is himself perfidious. That is not how the Court is run here. So I'm asking you again: What is your response to the allegation that you are a dangerous person and that, in general, your conduct generated the circumstances for violence? I am asking you the question. Forget that Mr. Nice asked you. I am putting it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whoever says about me that I am a wicked and dangerous man is an evil man, an underhand man, and a perfidious one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not getting anywhere, Mr. Seselj, and I have to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to let you know that you're not acting in the best interests of Mr. Milosevic, who has brought you here to assist him in his case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic brought me here to testify truthfully about the facts, upon the assumption that my truthful testimony about the facts could contribute to his Defence. And my response to Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have cut you off. I have cut you off. You must give a response which is devoid of any suggestion that relates to the character of the Prosecutor or that relates to my character or to the character of any member of the Bench. That is how adversarial proceedings are conducted and these are adversarial proceedings. If you do not have an answer to that, the Trial Chamber will instruct the Prosecutor to move to the next question and we will make a judgement. We will make our own decision as to the way you have responded or not responded. Mr. Nice, move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. And it may assist the witness in his deliberations, perhaps in respect of later questions, also to have in mind that by being confronted with the propositions that the Prosecution may argue in its closing arguments, he is being given an opportunity to meet them, which is only fair to him. If he chooses not to meet them, we will invite, of course, the inference that the proposition is well-founded. May we produce this document, then, that we've been asking questions about, give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What's the number for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand the numbering at this stage is not very clear and we'll get a number for that later. Can it be sorted out now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry about the messed up -- the document of this Ustasha -- Horvat's Ustasha Phantasmagorias should be 877, and the Politics as a Conscientious Challenge should be 876.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's probably been my fault for trying to short-circuit matters and I will take responsibility for dealing with each exhibit as we come to it. And the next one is a video clip for which there is a transcript being distributed. It comes from April 1991 and it's a Sanction clip, if the booth would like to be assisted by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There you are. That's the way you presented these arguments. Do you think that's an appeal to rational response or an appeal to passion in your audience?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I am a very passionate man, and I count upon human passions. But my speech before the war was held before the war in the form of a warning, a caution. I am in fact cautioning that there will be revenge if genocide against the Serb people is repeated. And that threat was stated publicly. It couldn't have been clearer than it was. But it was to have them deterred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say in the course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that last clip be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 878.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look now at another short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 878 was allotted to The Death of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you're right. Then it will be 879. But I didn't receive 878 yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now look at an excerpt from the programme, a short excerpt from the programme The Death of Yugoslavia, featuring this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware that the danger of propaganda lies in overstating the risks that people you wish to mobilise may be facing? Are you aware of that obvious problem with propaganda?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not propaganda at all. I'm talking about actual facts, and I did not exaggerate anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, where was that speech made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It was blurred, and I couldn't really see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems to me pretty basic to know where it was made and who you were speaking to. Can we get that clarified, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we can get it clarified immediately because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, these sort of TV broadcasts are just throw in a piece -- please, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can clarify it if they play it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Without reference as to where it is, it doesn't actually assist, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, help us: At what part of the 1990s were you urging your people on by reference to Ustasha hordes attacking Serbian villages?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you can see probably where the speech was made, and I heard some introduction in English, and that probably shows when and where. Judging by this particular footage, I think that it was made in Serbia, but I cannot remember each and every one of my speeches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, now they turned it on. I think it would be proper to interpret the English part of the text to Mr. Seselj too, and we did hear the soundtrack from the video footage that Mr. Nice had played.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm happy to play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very blurred, the image I see here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "[Voiceover]... set about provoking a conflict between Serbs and Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, then, that has to be, doesn't it, in 1990 or 1991, before the conflict starts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask, first of all, why the transcript that we have is different from what's on the screen? Is there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours may recall that with The Death of Yugoslavia and the programme itself, we often discovered that the programme subtitles were more a summary of what was said than a transcribed and interpreted version of what was said. So what you have is a transcribed version of the precise words and then translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the reason I'm asking you about this, Mr. Seselj, is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have an objection to what Mr. Nice said just now. He explains that in this BBC programme, in the subtitles, there is more of a summary. That is not true. What the subtitles present are brutal lies. You have seen forgeries of what I had said, and I told you that I noticed mistakes and then your interpreters here had it replayed for them five times and they interpreted it right. And very often, tendentiously, in The Death of Yugoslavia, the translation is a brutal lie and a falsification. Because they're counting on the fact that their audiences do not speak Serbian, and they don't care about the Serbs themselves. So this is worthless evidence. It's only evidence of the anti-Serb propaganda waged here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, then if we are to admit as evidence this transcript, it will have to be admitted subject to the qualification that you have made and which Mr. Milosevic has just emphasised. And it is also open to Mr. Milosevic to deal with the matter in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it would appear, would it, that this was in the federal parliament -- in front of the federal parliament in Belgrade, from what we can see, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly in front of the federal Assembly, judging by the big masses of people there. It is somewhere in Serbia. It was impossible to get this many people together at the rallies in Serb Krajina. It was in Serbia. Possibly it was the rally in front of the federal Assembly on the 15th or 21st of May, 1991. And I don't know what kind of image you have on your screens, but mine is highly blurred. It's highly blurred even now. Perhaps something can be done about this. It is totally blurred. The guard can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're only concerned in, not in a limited extent, but to a different extent, in what you were doing and why. We're more concerned in what effect this had for the responsibility of the accused. But you were allowed, without any complaint, to be addressing people on the basis that there were Ustasha hordes trying to finish up the genocide. Well, who were these Ustasha hordes that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustasha hordes are, first and foremost, members of Tudjman's ZNG, National Guards Corps, the paramilitary unit that attacked the Serb civilian population and all the Western Serbian lands within the Croatian federal unit. That's what Ustasha hordes are. Now, as for your position regarding the fact that I was allowed to do so, there was full freedom of speech in Serbia in Mr. Milosevic's time. Nobody could allow me or prevent me from presenting my opinion. According to the laws of Serbia, that is not a criminal offence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that clip with the printed transcript be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And the transcript subject to the qualification that I've made.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 880.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, who provided this transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was done by us. And I think it's -- well, it counts as a draft translation. It wasn't done by CLSS, but a lot of translations are draft, to that extent draft. It was done by us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May I suggest, because there have been problems over translations and the accuracy of them, that if video clips are being shown, that we have the booth here interpret the language so we get it on the transcript, and that avoid problems in what text was actually used. We have found, as Mr. Milosevic has raised, that the subtitles have been inaccurate. I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't hear any opposition in relation to this specific transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It may be better if we just play the clip again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Kay, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your interpretation is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... again so that we have a translation for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- the accused says this is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The position will remain as we had determined. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that clip can be exhibited and given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's 880, already given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the next one, please, is a short clip from a programme first, I think, screened in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you get this video monitor to work better before you proceed? It is very blurred. It is very hard for me to discern anything. Can a technician of yours come and see this, and they can see that it is very hard to follow this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's the angle you are watching from. So if you could stand up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can the monitor be inclined?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This one, Your Honours, was first screened in Serbian television. It was reproduced in a later programme called Pictures of Words and Hate, Year Two, produced by the television programme B92 in Belgrade. But it has the RTS logo on the footage, so that would indicate its original broadcast company. And I hope that the transcripts provided by us have been distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a specific reference, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's 23A, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's better. Can you see it now, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hardly. I can barely see it. Due to the microphones, I can only assume that this is the National Assembly. But your technician can come and see for himself. It is barely --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... stand to view these because I think it's just a matter of angle, unless his monitors are in some way deficient. I can see, on the monitors of the same kind that he has, a perfectly clear picture. But I think if you sit down, it goes down so you can hardly see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your technician is standing here, and he can tell you what is looks like on this screen. If he says that it can be seen fine, then I will accept it too. And whether it's a matter of getting up or sitting down or whether it's a question of image quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you were to -- well, the technician is coming, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that your own technician has told you that this was not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Remember, the picture is not going to be 100 per cent clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This image is not clear even 2 per cent. You can only see the silhouette of a white shirt, and nothing else, and the microphones in front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can't you see the face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Well, ask your technicians whether they can see it. Can they see anything here? Now it's somewhat better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Our thanks to the technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the transcripts to hand, as distributed, may this now be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The line between Karlobag-Ogulin-Virovitica has to be our goal and that is the line where the Yugoslav People's Army has to put its troops. If the army is unable to move the troops to this line peacefully from Zagreb then they should do this with force and with the bombing of Zagreb. The army still has capacities which it has not used yet. If its troops are endangered it has the right to use Napalm bombs and anything else they have available. We cannot play games here. It is more important to save one army than to worry if there will be some accidental victims. Who is to blame here? They wanted war, so now they have it."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Seselj said very clearly that this is a line where the army has to withdraw its troops, and the word used here is to "put" its troops, as if it were coming from somewhere and putting its troops there. The army is withdrawing from Croatia and he uses the word twice, to "withdraw" its troops to that line. Once again, this is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. That's a very bad mistake. Let's play it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is the only way it makes sense, I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the interpreters could interpret as the text -- as the words --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is very hard for the interpreters to follow the soundtrack as it is spoken if they're interpreting. They cannot get everything in. Perhaps, if you like, we can listen to this particular word if we hear it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the word used was to "withdraw" troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is in the parliament, so this is you in a slightly more restrained mode; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is in the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, sometime in the beginning of July 1991. I'm speaking here as an opposition MP and presenting my political views.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And amongst other things at this stage, advocating the right to use napalm?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am advocating the withdrawal of JNA troops from Croatia, from Zagreb, first and foremost, and other towns, and that that withdrawal should be carried out even if it involves fighting. To use all the means they have available in order to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, identifying the Karlobag line as the line from which troops should be withdrawn; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Since the Croat paramilitary forces are attacking all barracks in Croatia, I'm asking in a timely manner for the JNA to withdraw from Croatia to the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica line. Unfortunately, no one heeded or accepted my call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you put that as identifying the line as the line from which, but it's the line to which.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the sense is clear. May that be exhibited as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 881.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I have a few more on the same topic before we turn to another topic. Can we look now, please, at what, for the interpreters, will be 23B and is a copy of part of one of your magazines, or your newspapers. This one published in 1992, I think. And for the Court, it's the second sheet, page marked 29. At some stage the whole document was translated but you haven't been--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the last one, before we move on from it, has a date September 1991 at the top of it. What does that date refer to? Is this when it was broadcast as a compilation in some --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no, no. This was the original date of broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the witness has given evidence that it was in June 1991, so you ought to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. We can look at this document. This is from Velika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document we're now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was elected only in June as a member of parliament. It could not have been in June, it could have been only in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. It was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So what we're now looking at, please, is I think perhaps published in 1991, but when you look at it, you may be able to help us, if you look at the original. It's November 1991, I think. And the outlined passage on our page 29 in the text says: "Today, dear Gradimir, as we say goodbye to you on your final journey -" perhaps you can find that in the outlined text - "we can repeat our Serbian and Chetnik pledge you will not remain unavenged! Our enemies will feel the punishment of the Serbian people. We shall no longer forgive as we did after World War I and World War II. The time has come to settle old scores... to avenge all Serbian victims and to unite all the Serbian lands." By statements like this in the publications that you produced, are you generating hate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have the factual basis, first of all? Is it in a publication, and what's the date of the publication?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can identify this as from your own magazine, Velika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was published in the newspaper Velika Srbija, sometime in the summer of 1991. It is number 11, not the 11th month, as Mr. Nice thought. Then I published the text again in my book the Serb Chetnik Movement, in 1994. This is a speech of mine, made on the 27th of August, at Mount Cemernik, in the village of Pavletina, in an area that is called Crna Trava - this is the south of Serbia - at the funeral of the first volunteer of the Serb Radical Party who got killed, Gradimir Pesic. In order to understand the context, I demand that the entire speech be read out. It's not long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A matter for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic can have that done in re-examination. That's one of the purposes of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have this document exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But my question to you is this: By these sorts of words, and we've probably come to the end of a sufficient example of this particular type of topic, were you not simply doing your best to generate hate that would lead to violence?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not disseminating hate. I am talking about Serb foes. You know what foe, enemy, means in the Serbian language. The word is "dusmanin," but it comes from the Arabic or Persian language. That is the worst enemy of all. That is the worst enemy of all, the dusmanin is. That's the one who wants to destroy your very essence, the essence of your nation. The word is used to refer to Ustashas. That's quite clear. As for the reference to the First and Second World War, in the Second World War, the top Ustasha leaders, with the assistance of the Catholic Church, through the well-known rat channels of the Vatican, fled from Croatia to South America. Books were written about that. They all remained unpunished. This time, I am saying that no one should remain unpunished. Revenge is punishment for the perpetrators of genocidal crimes. But not in a single text of mine will you find anything like having to kill Croat civilians. You won't find that anywhere. In the Second World War, just think of all the terms that the British and the Americans used for Germans. They said that they were Huns, they were barbarians, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And perhaps one more moment and then I'll move to another topic, I think, to look at the other side of what you were doing, I'm going to suggest to you. Can we look at 23C.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Exhibit number for the previous exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it 881 or 882?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It should be 882.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The exhibit that's -- potential exhibit that's being distributed has not been marked with the text, so I'll withdraw it for the time being, ask you to lay it on one side. Otherwise, it will take too much time finding the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the short position is, Mr. Seselj, that over the period of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time we've been looking at or focussing on, you were drawing to people's attention the suffering of Serbs historically, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was incessantly drawing people's attention to the suffering of the Serb people through history, especially the suffering of the Serb people in contemporary times, when I myself was an observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were categorising basically all Croats as Ustasha. You hardly distinguished between, as it were, the good and the bad; they were all Ustasha, lumped together.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. You yourself quoted a text of mine yesterday where I actually praised the true Croats who still lived in Istria, Kvarner, Rijeka, where there were no persecutions of Serbs. In the first half of 1991, practically throughout Croatia, the systematic persecution of the Serb people started and hundreds and thousands of Serbs already started fleeing to Serbia. I bear in mind yet another fact, that there was mass Ustasha hysteria in Croatia at the time, similar like in 1941. I would like to draw your attention to historical testimony provided by eyewitnesses, that the Croats in Zagreb welcomed Hitler's troops in 1941 with more enthusiasm and delight than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from praising those people who you defined as Croats because they lived in the two bits of Croatia that you were prepared to accept as being Croatia, am I right that you were categorising the left basically as all Ustasha and generating emotion by doing that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct that I was categorising the rest of the Croats as all Ustasha. However, I am telling you that mass Ustasha hysteria prevailed in the largest part of Croatia. And at one point, most Croats actually declared that they were adherents of the Ustasha Tudjman regime, it had become so powerful in Croatia. And that's what I was warning the Serb public about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I cannot find this, but I don't know what Mr. Nice is referring to. This is a large text, some 50 or so pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That text has been withdrawn. Is that the text headed "A guest of radio --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right. I'm just identifying the passages I want to ask about and I may come back to it. And I've got one more question to ask this witness before I do. I think I can find the text in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's one side, the emotions you're generating. So far as on the other side is concerned, Croats and then, later, Muslims, your concern was to make them fear the consequences of what was to come, and so far as the Muslims was concerned, your intention was to make them think they would be booted out of the country in certain circumstances; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that the Muslims could or should be booted out of the country. In the year 1990, I wrote an appeal to the Serbs of the Islamic faith, which I started with the words "Brother Muslims." I exerted my utmost efforts to avoid a war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, like the one that had broken out in Croatia. However, I constantly attack Islamic fundamentalists and pan-Islamists. And I am not stirring up emotions of that kind; I am simply warning that the crimes against the Serb people in Croatia are being repeated and taking the same form they had taken in World War II. I was bearing in mind, at the same time, that a Croatian member of parliament spoke in the Croatian parliament - we all saw this on television - and he ended his speech with the old Ustasha greeting, which was exactly the same as Hitler's and Mussolini's greeting had been. And he was speaking in the Croatian parliament. You think you can pull things out of context, but every speech of mine is a response to even worse things that were happening in Croatia. In the Croatian parliament, an MP came forward and raised his arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll now turn to the last document we're looking at in this passage, and perhaps it can be either distributed or picked up - I think I can deal with it - and made available to the witness. And if he'd like to look at the Serbian version and at the cover page, he can tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a document headed "A Guest of Radio Index."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd like to look at the front page of the Serbian version, Mr. Seselj, remind yourself of what this document is.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my book entitled "Through the Political Galimatias." This is a collection of my radio and television broadcasts, and it was first published in 1993 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two passages I want you to look at. In the English it's at page 20, at the foot. And I think in the Serbian, Mr. Seselj, if you'd go, please, to what is page 263. I think this is the right passage. Would you start --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing is marked on that page for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, would you just read the first -- go to the foot of 263 and see the paragraph there. There's maybe an additional paragraph that I want to ask you about. And would you just read the first three words of that paragraph so I can make sure I'm in the right place.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Television is the most powerful medium. It's a very dangerous medium..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you now just please read on and we can follow it in the English. "It is a very dangerous..."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Television is the most powerful. It is a very dangerous weapon, too, and this was evident in the West. Television can be a source of a much more dangerous type of totalitarianism than Fascism and Communism combined, those who rule television rule human thoughts and emotions. On television, controlling two or three television companies, you can serve up political standpoints to all citizens of America, you can simply shape their minds, their behaviour and so forth. This is very dangerous but it calls for far more studious scientific approaches."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You therefore recognised the potential for television. At the time with which we are concerned, what influence do you say the accused had over those who ran the major television stations?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little influence. He could have influenced only one television station, and that's ETS, the state television of Serbia, because the editor-in-chief and director of that television station was a member of his party. All the others were their competitors and opposed Mr. Milosevic. That is a very different situation from the one prevailing in America. All Western television stations, in unison, were waging an anti-Serb policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a difference in your access to television, depending on how the state of your relationship was with this accused? When you were in favour with him, you were allowed access to television; when you were out of favour, you were denied it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in favour or out of favour with Mr. Milosevic. We had periods of cooperation which were much shorter than our periods of deep conflict. At those times when we were not in conflict, I and the Serb Radical Party appeared on the state-run television more often. However, our presence on other television stations did not depend on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when you appeared on state-run television, as you explain and as we've heard in evidence from other witnesses, more often when you were not in conflict with the accused, he didn't restrain you, did he, in any way as to the things you might say? He allowed you to say whatever you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday, Mr. Nice, that I am not a horse for Mr. Milosevic to rein me in. Whoever appeared on state-run television was free to express his opinions. I appeared far less on state-run television than other opposition politicians. On the state-run television, these were most often duels, debates, and round tables. No one ever suggested to anyone else what they should say, or prohibit them from saying anything. The broadcasts were aired live. I never agreed to pre-record a broadcast. There were attempts to make me agree to that, but I always refused. I only agreed to participate in shows that were broadcast live.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next passage I want to refer to, which is marked, and the Chamber will find it -- you've got it on page 266, Mr. Seselj. If the Chamber would be good enough to go to the top of page 26, or possibly the bottom of page 25, I think. You'll find a passage, a paragraph there, Mr. Seselj, that begins with: "As for the Krajina, if the Bosnian Serbs capitulate..." Can you find that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if you go on in that paragraph to what we can find on our page 26 and you'll see marked, you say this: "And these Serbs, our folk, cannot stay in the Islamic Jamahirija either, nor in Tudjman's Ustasha Croatia, they are certain to be expelled if not killed. Serbs are now fighting for their survival and in this fight they have run out of options, the alternative is either capitulation or total victory. If they resist, they have a chance of winning, and if they capitulate they will lose everything." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Winding up the emotions or not?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot understand that the translator first says, Do you see this passage, and then corrects him or herself and says "interpreter's correction." How can such a mistake be made? In both cases, my response is "yes." But how can the interpreter falsify the question in this way? It could have been something more sensitive. It could have been something where my answer would have been "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, there is no basis at all, as you must know, for suggesting that the interpreter is falsifying the question. If a mistake is made by the interpreter, then so be it. Why must you attribute ill motives to the interpreter? Let's move on. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that be exhibited. The first passage provided particularly interesting and the rest of it may become valuable. May that be given an exhibit?.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 883.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's now turn then to a different topic, but again at this stage through the things you have been saying. Can we have 25A-5, please. I'm looking now, Mr. Seselj, at things that you said, in particular insofar as they reveal acts of those named as co-perpetrators. Let's go to 25A-1. This is -- 25A-1, for the interpreters, who have the materials. This is part of an existing exhibit, 469, tab 3, a meeting of the Council for the Coordination of Positions of State Policy. Now, were you aware of the existence of something called the Council of Coordinating Positions of State Policy?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a body we've heard about. It met in the course of 1993, certainly, I think 1992, 1993. And this one was from a meeting held on the 21st of January of 1993, involving, amongst others, this accused and Radovan Karadzic, but many others as well; Mladic, for example. Now, have you got the document in front of you? You'll see that the evidence before the Court --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More than once I warned Mr. Nice, and you here, not to twist the explanation of this Council for Coordination of Positions of State Policy. It was established by the then president, Dobrica Cosic, and its members were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear the question that Mr. Nice has to put in relation to this council, and then if you have an objection, then you may raise it. We haven't heard the question yet, so you're premature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, given the difficulties there have been with interpretation and translation, where an original text in Serbian exists, it may be better to ask the witness to read it out, even though it's not his own words, if the Court is happy with this, and we can follow the translation, the interpretation, and hear it against the translation we already have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness should know what he is reading from. He cannot have page 21 taken out of the transcript of some kind of minutes that he knows nothing about and then be told to read out a sentence. I think that is completely improper, and I don't think that this is the way in which Mr. Nice can present evidence here. Let him bring the minutes from that meeting so that he can see who the members of this body are, who was invited, what was discussed, and then he can read out a sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let us hear the question. Let us hear the question first. That's how we will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, whether the witness reads it or not, perhaps I'll read it this time and we'll see how we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'll see here Karadzic is recorded as saying this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of your page 20 and it's on page 21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bear in mind that we don't have it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't have it? It's on the overhead projector. That's right. It's an existing exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it 469, tab 3? Because I'm looking at 469, tab 3 and don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 39. My apologies if I read out tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what Karadzic said is this: "I think that this which Jovanovic is talking about has already happened, to a huge extent. There was 50/50 of us in Zvornik. The number of inhabitants in Zvornik is now the same, approximately 50.000, and they are all Serbs. More than 24.000 Serbs from Zenica and Central Bosnia have arrived and stopped in Zvornik. If only Serbia would help us by not accepting refugees, which it does not have to accept, and returned them, that would be a great solution. For example, if all the people from Western Slavonia --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have to move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page, top of the page, Mr. Nort. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "-- and returned them, that would be a great solution. For example, if all the people from Western Slavonia were to return and all those from the former Bosnia and Herzegovina who are in Serbia, people from Doboj, Derventa, Odzak, et cetera, that would be the factual state of affairs which nobody could change any more. Not only should the military conscripts be returned, but the families should as well, to locations where there is no war and where freedom exists." First and generally, is there anything in what Karadzic said that you disagree with factually?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have we identified the occasion on which this statement was made?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is from the meeting of the 21st of January, 1993, and it's an existing exhibit and it's the Council for Coordinating Positions on State Policy, sometimes described as the Council for Harmonisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, is there anything in what I've read out to you with which you disagree, factually, coming from the mouth of Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you have given me no evidence that Karadzic really said this. Even if this meeting was held, I did not attend it. I don't know if Karadzic attended it or whether he said this. You have not given me the entire document either. You should ask the people who allegedly participated in this meeting about this. As for the facts, what is there for me to confirm or deny here? What facts are these? Allegedly, he is expressing his positions, not facts. There are no particular facts here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Seselj, from the Prosecutor is whether you disagree with that position as expressed by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether Karadzic said this at all. I can neither agree or disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you can assume that he said it. Assuming that he said it, do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What should I agree to? Can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, put it more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you're having difficulty with seeing the factual content of this passage, just tell us this: Were you involved in events at Zvornik in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in any events in Zvornik in 1992. But volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were, as part of the JNA, at the very beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make any speeches in respect of events that happened in Zvornik in 1992? To encourage your troops, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not visit Zvornik or give any speeches there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But nevertheless, troops of the Serb Radical Party were there and you must have known what happened, because you told us you --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what's described here is a complete change of the ethnic composition of Zvornik from 50/50 to 100 per cent Serb, first of all, and this is the factual part of what Karadzic was saying. Was he right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there were no troops of the Serb Radical Party there, nor did the Serb Radical Party ever have any troops of its own. The volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were in Zvornik, but as part of the JNA, while the JNA was still there. As for the ethnic make-up of the population of Zvornik, according to my knowledge, before the war, there really were approximately half Serbs, half Muslims, more or less. However, during the war, many Muslims left Zvornik. Serb refugees from areas under Muslim control moved into Zvornik. That is a fact, yes. And I can testify about those facts. But I cannot say whether Radovan Karadzic actually said this or not. You are trying to tender this document through me as if I was confirming that he said this and that I agreed with him. Had I agreed with Karadzic, we would have been members of the same party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find it constantly frustrating when you don't answer the question. You have now answered this question, and you've answered it very well and very clearly. And what I find difficult to understand is why you constantly misinterpret what's being asked of you. This is already a document which is exhibited in the case. It's not being exhibited through you. You're simply being asked whether these facts as set out in this document are accurate. At no stage have you been asked to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. confirm whether Karadzic said it or not. So please listen carefully to the questions you're being asked and answer the question you're actually being asked, and we'll get on far better and far more quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, when a precise question is asked of me, I give a very precise answer. If the question is about the ethnic make-up of the population of Zvornik, I can answer to the best of my knowledge. But these two pieces of paper represent no kind of document, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall simply have to differ on whether you actually do answer the questions that you're asked. Please try to do so, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain, from your broad knowledge of events, then, how it came about that 50 per cent Muslim population of a town like Zvornik suddenly disappears -- not suddenly, but over a short period of time disappears?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Nice's question is improper because Seselj did not say that 50 per cent of the inhabitants of Zvornik went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I think you understand what I've asked you. Will you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in Zvornik, some crimes were committed, as far as I know. Some of these crimes were tried in 1993, and trials for some of them are now being held in Belgrade. And for some, trials have yet to be held. So I'm not excluding the possibility that there were crimes. However, the vast majority of the Muslim population left Zvornik. Some came to Serbia. Some crossed the River Drina to Mali Zvornik, where they had friends and relatives who were also Muslims and where they felt safe. I assume most went to Muslim-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, this is a perfect example, because the question was: What caused this to happen? And you haven't addressed that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What could have been the possible reasons? First of all, the atmosphere of war. Before the war, many people left Zvornik, both Serbs and Muslims. During the war, many Muslim civilians withdrew when their paramilitary formations withdrew. Some crossed over into Serbia. Some, after the fighting in Zvornik, left Zvornik and went to territories under Muslim control. That's how I see what happened. If your question is whether some of them were expelled, perhaps they were. I don't exclude that possibility. Some Muslims may have been expelled, but which ones? As far as I know, it was certainly not the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then who? You see, you've claimed the broadest knowledge, and when it's -- on many occasions the most detailed knowledge of all events on the accused's indictment. You tell us that you've read broadly. Here a population changes its ethnic composition completely. Who drove these people out?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying once again that most of them were not expelled. Some of them might have been expelled, but I wasn't there so I cannot testify about it. You want me to say so-and-so expelled Muslims from there. If I knew that, I'd tell you right away. I know a little bit about the Yellow Wasps. I might know something about some other paramilitary units in certain places, but as for every detail that happened in Zvornik, I can't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You claim this omniscience and omnipresence, in many ways, certainly omniscience. Who would have been directing paramilitaries to drive people from Zvornik? Please help us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean that some factor of the authorities led them to do so, then I don't believe that. But you know full well that the paramilitary formations were usually ordinary criminal gangs. So the general mood that prevailed was such that paramilitaries could perhaps have influenced people and made them leave, and things like that did happen. But concretely speaking, specifically speaking, Zvornik, you're asking me to answer the impossible and you once again claim that I am saying that I know everything, that I am omniscient. Only God knows everything. I know far, far less than him. I know more than you, but that of course doesn't mean that I know everything myself. And now you're asking me to testify about something that I have absolutely no knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've told us in your own evidence about the danger of paramilitary formations. We've heard about the power of television, through your own words. And we know from evidence in this Court that circumstances can come together to allow the most terrible crimes, genocidal and other, to be committed in various locations as a result of what politicians and others do at the top. If, as you say, it was free-floating paramilitary groups that kicked half the population of Zvornik out, or whatever percentage it did remove, who had been creating the atmosphere in which that could happen, Mr. Seselj? Was it you? Was it this accused? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, and once again, you are misinterpreting what I said. It is not that the majority of Muslims were expelled from Zvornik. I don't exclude the possibility, of course, that some of them were expelled, just as some of them were killed. I don't think we can challenge those facts that there were Muslims civilians who were indeed killed. However, the majority left, for different reasons. Many left before the war, like the Serbs did. The mood was such that prevailed them to do so. Some of them withdrew with their paramilitaries. Some of them left later on. But what this process was in specific terms, how do you expect me to testify to that? And then you misinterpret it and say everybody was expelled or the majority was expelled. I just don't believe that. And I state this: There were situations where incidents took place, there was killing, there was looting, there was persecution. Now, as far as the paramilitary formations are concerned, once the JNA had withdrawn, you know, this is what happened. The situation with respect to the functioning of power was fairly chaotic at the time and this kind of situation creates conditions conducive to the appearance of paramilitary formations because criminals want to make use of the war situation for their criminal aspirations. So there's no doubt on that score. And somebody even from the authorities could have been in cohorts with the paramilitary formations. But I can't give you specific facts about that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How should I know who? From the local authorities, perhaps. I'm just guessing now. You're making me guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, staying, for a few minutes, with Zvornik, you know from the pre-trial brief served in your case, because you dealt with this in part, I think in your own evidence, that a witness or potential witness called (redacted) says that you gave a speech at Mali Zvornik in the spring of 1992, saying words to the effect of: "Dear Chetnik brothers across the Drina, you are the bravest ones. We are going to clean Bosnia of pagans and show them a road which will take them to the East, where they belong." Now, tell us: Did you make a speech in Mali Zvornik, across the Drina, in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, at the beginning of 1992, I was at a church near Mali Zvornik when it was being consecrated. But I can't remember what period of time that was exactly. A long time before the war, at any rate. But that witness is a false witness, because I never said that in any of my speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there anything that you might have said by way of encouraging the Serbs across the river in Zvornik itself?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have been. As far as I remember, there was a problem there already because some Serb taxi-driver had been killed. So possibly I was speaking about that. But then you should have my whole speech and not somebody's false interpretation, untruthful. But quite certainly, I couldn't have called anybody in Bosnia a pagan. That is absolutely impossible. I'm not as stupid as that. I'm not as uneducated as that to be able to do so. And that would have been completely wrong. I would have turned out an idiot had I said that they were pagans because Islam is a monotheistic religion, is much more monotheistic than Christianity itself is. In Islam there's just one God and there's no Holy Trinity, there are no saints or anything else. So it would have been impossible for me to have said something like that, absolutely impossible. But I could have attacked the pan-Islamists who wished Bosnia-Herzegovina to secede from Yugoslavia. That is all quite possible. But then you would have had to have had the original speech. What your false witness is saying is absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's so many books of yours, it's not possible to research them in the way that might be desirable. Can you remember whether you've published anywhere a speech of yours given in Mali Zvornik in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have many books, but it is possible to look into them all. You have the resources. At present, I don't have the resources to delve in that study. But in principle, all speeches which any of my associates recorded, I published. There might have been some speech that wasn't recorded and therefore not made public, not published. For example, I had a television programme in Leskovac, in the south of Serbia, in Bojnjak, the place name was, I believe, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two preliminary questions for you before I show you a little bit of a videotape. You sent your volunteers, or your volunteers were sent, or whatever happened, to go to Zvornik, which is across the Drina. What were they going there to do?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were sent as soldiers of the JNA, as volunteers in JNA units. And before they were sent, I didn't know that they were going to Zvornik at all. They went where the command of the JNA thought they ought to be deployed. And we were just told the wishes, that is to say, how many volunteers and when they were supposed to arrive in the Bubanj Potok barracks, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many volunteers were required?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who. Someone from the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't you know who asked you for your volunteers to be sent?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, it's like this: We had a wartime staff in the Serb Radical Movement and at the head of that staff was my vice-president and he went in my name to the General Staff to reach an agreement. And on the basis of that, the volunteers were convened. I didn't deal with these technical matters. But behind the sending of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party was me, I myself, as president of the party. But there are technical details of how many, when and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... comes from the soldier and not the General Staff. I mean, for example, no politician could ever have been involved in a request for volunteers to be sent to Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a single politician. My vice-president, Ljubisa Petkovic, whose statement you have, contacted the General Staff and mostly his contacts were with General Domazetovic. And he would report to me from time to time about those contacts. But not all the technical details, because that wasn't essential. The essential thing was that the General Staff would tell us their wishes and needs and requirements, and within the frameworks of our possibilities, we would bring in volunteers from various parts of Serbia, even Montenegro, and we would send them where the General Staff told us to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... ask you for volunteers to be sent?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Radmilo Bogdanovic, the former minister of the interior; is that who you mean? Bogdanovic. I don't know another Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the accused wouldn't ask you for the volunteers to be sent, would he?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another little matter that you might help us with before we look at the piece of footage I want you to review with us is this: The Red Berets, just define for us what you say they were.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Berets were of different types, different types of units who wore red berets on their heads. So only that concept would be the right kind of concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there ever a particular unit commanded by a particular person that was known as the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A unit with the official name of the Red Berets did not exist. What did exist were different units whose members wore red berets. The ones who were in Golubic in the Captain Dragan training centre and I clashed with them and I attacked them publicly, I already told you that in Republika Srpska I found in a judgement there -- in the judgement of this tribunal that in several places mention is made of a reconnaissance or intervention platoon of the Red Berets within the Bratunac Brigade, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us about a unit that was formed in 1996, I think. Now, what was that all about? Was that the Red Berets or something like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did have in the public -- or rather, the people called them the Red Berets, but their official title was the Unit for Special Operations of the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Under the control of?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the control of the State Security Service of Serbia. And I think the first commander was Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the first commander was Franko Simatovic, nicknamed Frenki, if I remember well. And then after that, it was Milorad Lukovic, known as Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he and his unit first sprung into being or came into being in 1996 and not a day before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Franko Simatovic, Frenki, did not begin to exist in 1996. He existed prior to that. And to the best of my knowledge, he was even a volunteer in Srpska Krajina. But I can't say for sure where, because I never saw him. I never met him until he came to the prison here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... question and we'll go back to it and I'll rephrase it. Did the formal unit, headed by Simatovic, exist only in 1996 or did it exist before 1996?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That unit existed only as of 1996 onwards. The people who joined it in 1996 were mostly war veterans who had fought previously. Some of them were with Captain Dragan. Others were Arkan's Tigers. Quite possibly there were some volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party, although no name comes to mind just now. And there were some other people too who made a name for themselves in the war. And the object was to select the best fighters, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please don't fall into the trap of giving the answer you think is wanted of you. Just think about this: Given your positions, your role with your own party and your relationship with this accused and so on, is there any possibility that you could have been kept in the dark, kept ignorant, of the existence of a special unit under Simatovic between 1991 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, nobody had the duty of informing me, because I wasn't a man in authority. I was an opposition politician. Secondly, I make a clear distinction between the Red Berets, formed in 1996, and various other units who were known popularly by that name which had existed earlier. From the very beginning, Captain Dragan wore a red beret and that's what his men were referred to as. And I even clashed with him and attacked them publicly because of certain things. And you'll be able to find that in some of my books.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll try to give you an opportunity to consider it really calmly and take moments for reflection if you need to. I'll ask you the question again. Is there any possibility that you could have been kept in the dark, kept ignorant, of the existence of a special unit under Simatovic that existed between 1991 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
