utterances.text: First of all -- well, I'm very calm, so what you're saying is no good to you at all. Nobody had the duty of informing me about anything. That's the first point. Especially not giving me information of that nature. To the best of my knowledge, Franko Simatovic, Frenki, was a volunteer in Krajina, and to the best of my knowledge, he was the commander of some unit over there. However, I never met him until he came here to the prison. I knew about him, I had heard of him, and very often I attacked him, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have just one question about volunteers. Did the Socialist Party of Serbia have a structure for providing volunteers for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge, no, never. To the best of my knowledge, the Socialist Party of Serbia never dealt in providing and assembling volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this was a feature of parties which had more nationalist tendencies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only that. Nationalist and oppositional as well. But they could have been parties of a mass character. The Socialist Party of Serbia, however, in my opinion, was a party of a bureaucratic nature. You see, it included the white collar workers of the state, the authorities. It had sort of inherited power, a party which had inherited power from the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and the Socialist Alliance, when it was disbanded, to become the party of Serbia. Then the same cadres which were already in the state structures, mostly, I say, continued working within the Socialist Party. So it wasn't a party in the sense of being a spontaneous, mass party, such as the opposition parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would it be wrong of me to think it strange that a political party should be charged with or take on board the duty of organising volunteers for the army, the army of the federal republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not strange if you bear the situation in mind, the situation that the state was in at the time. The situation was highly confusing, chaotic, and the response to mobilisation in Serbia was pretty low, the mobilisation as pursued by the JNA, for ideological reasons. And we, in some way, tried to break up the ideological taboos that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, going back to the Red Berets, you actually know the Red Berets as a unit under Simatovic existed from 1991, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, Franko Simatovic was a volunteer over there for a time, and he was linked to that training centre of Captain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Dragan's in Golubic. And the people who had passed through that training centre had on their heads red berets, and for that reason they were called that way. There were even some cases when, from time to time, our volunteers were sent there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And do you know, from what you told us yourself in evidence in chief, that to create something like a paramilitary organisation in 1991, disturbing the proper holders of power and the proper what's called monopoly of violence, police and the army, disturbing that monopoly, is something that was never proper for this accused to do. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it is essential for the Defence of this accused to try and establish that no such unit was formed in 1991, because there would be no excuse for it, and that is why I'm going to suggest to you you're being entirely dishonest with the Court when you say you didn't know it existed.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state that it is you who are completely dishonest, Mr. Nice, and I also claim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do not persist in that kind of answer. It is perfectly proper for Mr. Nice to put to you that you are dishonest. It is not, on the other hand, proper for you to suggest that Mr. Nice is dishonest. He's putting his case to you, and you must appreciate the difference. On the basis of the instructions that he has and on the basis of the evidence in the trial, he's putting to you that your answer is dishonest. So answer that without suggesting that Mr. Nice is dishonest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to every abuse by Mr. Nice, I will respond in like kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you do that, if you do not answer the question that is properly put to you, we will move to the next question, and it will be for the Chamber to draw whatever inference is appropriate in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know if it will help or not, Mr. Seselj, to make this comment, but I'll make it anyway in the hope that it does. One crucial difference between a politician and a lawyer who presents a case in court is that politicians express personal opinions, and lawyers presenting cases in court don't. They make propositions based on evidence and argument -- as a foundation for argument that will arise later. And if there is a foundation somewhere in the evidence in this case which has gone on, as you know, since February 2002, for the proposition that the lawyer makes, then he's entitled to do it. If you were to respond like any other responsible witness, you would respect that, just as you would expect us to respect the way in which politicians undertake their exchanges. So I hope you will be able to answer the questions which are put perfectly properly in a constructive manner. Because only then will you be assisting the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, rephrase the question. And if we do not get an answer to it, then we'll move on. And as I said, it will be for the Chamber to draw whatever inference is appropriate in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The issue has been explained time and again to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question to you is this: It is essential for the Defence of this accused to try and establish that no such unit, that's the Red Berets under Simatovic, was formed in 1991. It's essential to do that, because as you've conceded, there could be no excuse for creating such a unit. And that is the foundation for my suggestion to you that you're being entirely dishonest with this Court when you assert that you didn't know it existed.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you are a completely dishonourable man, perfidious, and a liar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have to make the point that it's still obvious from the beginning that the witness would attempt to deflect attention by personalising issues. He will carry on doing it as long as he thinks it's in his interest, I suppose. Can I have a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the interpreters, I'm going to run through four video clips; 25B, C, D, and E. In each case, they come from the interview with this witness prepared for The Death of Yugoslavia film. In each case I think they are re-translations. But, Your Honours, we know the difficulties we've encountered, difficulties the interpreters have understandably encountered. Can I propose this as a solution: That we listen to the tape with the new translation in our hands, and if the interpreters are not able, as I suspect will be the case, to interpret as they're going along, if they can draw to our attention any errors that they perceive in the translation, and then I can ask questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we could distribute the first one, which comes from this interview. As there's no text on the actual monitor, or there's no text on the video film, someone, I think, should read -- if one of the interpreters would read the translation that has been distributed. And if they're not able to correct it as it's going along, if we could ask them if there are corrections at the end. I'll try that as a method, with the Court's leave. Ms. Dicklich suggests - and this may be a very useful proposal - that if I pause after a couple of sentences, or pause the tape and check for corrections at that stage, that would be better. I see nods from the booth. So if Ms. Dicklich could play this, please. It's in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they cannot hear the soundtrack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The soundtrack, at the moment is the question from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] In 1990 we were not acquiring weapons, we were only enlisting volunteers, and occasionally, when necessary, from time to time, we would send them to the front, but those were all very small groups. In 1991, we began organising volunteers on a larger scale and sending them to already established front lines, particularly to eastern Slavonia - here in the east of the Republic of Serb Krajina. Our volunteers..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having paused at that sentence, I don't know if I can check whether there's any correction to the transcript so far.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As far as the interpreters could hear - it is very fast - it was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Press on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Our volunteers distinguished themselves especially at the battle in Borovo Selo, which took place on May 2nd, 1991, when they defeated the stronger Croatian forces - Croatian police and para-police forces. We were getting..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, that sentence, any corrections?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As far as we could hear, it was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. Press on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] We were getting weapons from Milosevic's police, from the then -- first from the then Foreign -- Minister of Internal Affairs Radmilo Bogdanovic, and then when he was replaced, from his successor. We were getting old weapons from the warehouse of the Territorial Defence. There were old American Thompson guns, which had been withdrawn from use long time ago. Then there were old M-48 guns, the so-called Tandzare.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That passage?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As far as we could hear, it was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the last passage, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Therefore, it was pretty much everything that was obsolete, what the army had stopped using a long time ago, what was kept somewhere in the warehouses of the Territorial Defence. They felt sorry to destroy it all, so they just gave them to us. But it was with those weapons that we beat the modernly equipped Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in the course of that answer to Laura Silber on The Death of Yugoslavia tape, you said that you were getting weapons from Milosevic's police, from the then Minister of Internal Affairs, Radmilo Bogdanovic, and then from his successor. True or false?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This entire interview, which lasted about one hour, is one I published in one of my books. And you could have found that too. So I'm not challenging the fact that I gave this interview, however, for reasons of political propaganda, I threw Mr. Milosevic and Radmilo Bogdanovic into the entire story, wanting to annoy them and to cause on their part an improper political reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm going to make this proposition once, although it is going to apply to the remaining passages we're going to look at. This account that you're giving of lying to Laura Silber on these particular topics that you mentioned in your evidence in chief is something you and the accused know you have to say to get round the revelations that come from these tapes, and you're lying to the Court in saying that you said these things about Milosevic and Bogdanovic for the reasons you've just given, in 1995. Do you understand me? This is all part of an intent to mislead this Court when you say you were lying to Laura Silber.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there is nothing that I have to wiggle my way out of here. I'm proud of the volunteers in Borovo Selo, the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, and to the end of my life, I will remain proud of that. Secondly, the weapons were found in the village when the volunteers arrived. As I was engaged in a propaganda war against Mr. Milosevic, every time I spoke in public I tried to draw him into something that he would find most uncomfortable. Also, the regime was fighting a propaganda war against me in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm giving you opportunity to deal with these things in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask: In what way would that make Mr. Milosevic feel uncomfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because at that time Mr. Milosevic had very good relations with the Western powers. He accepted Western peace initiatives, purportedly peace initiatives, and also there was the Vance-Owen Plan and all the way up to the beginning of 1998, that was the period of time just before the Dayton agreement. When was this TV show actually -- or rather, when was this interview made? Mr. Nice can help out with that. I think it was on the eve of the Dayton agreement. So why was I saying all of this? In order to harm Mr. Milosevic politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In March 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is an example, then, of bombast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. In March 1995, I had just got out of prison, that Mr. Milosevic's authorities had put me into. I left on the 30th of January, or rather, the 29th of January was when I was released. I was released from prison with a couple of thousand people. I passed by the seat of the Presidency of Serbia, where Mr. Milosevic was sitting, and I made a speech. And I attacked him with the worst possible vocabulary, whatever crossed my mind. Whatever my imagination gave me, I said against Mr. Milosevic in those days. And I was always mindful of using whatever might harm him the most politically, in view of his political positions. If you look at my speeches from that period, from 1995, you will find a great many of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, bear in mind that the reference here is to events in 1991. Now, a lot happened in Yugoslavia between 1991 and 1995. How could this account, which would show to the Serbian people Mr. Milosevic assisting in a successful campaign in 1991, how could that be seen to be to your political advantage and to his political disadvantage in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's very logical: I am giving an interview to a BBC journalist. Her bosses sent her to Serbia to collect material for the TV programme of theirs that had God knows how many installments. I am repeating something that the Western media and the anti-Serb media at home were saying in the propaganda campaign in 1991, 1992, and 1993. In mid-1993, they stopped their propaganda campaign. Then I highlighted all these arguments that had already been presented. Everything that I said in 1995 against Mr. Milosevic is what you can find in the Western media and the anti-Serb media in Serbia over the previous years. They stopped that, but I kept grinding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lower the volume and reduce the speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that same year, 1995, I went to prison again. Sometime around the 2nd of June, I was arrested in Gnjilane and sent to prison with my associates for about two months. Mr. Milosevic's government sent me to prison and I made speeches that had to be the most uncomfortable for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, maybe you can't help me, but you didn't answer the question at all just now. Because I was anxious to know how this would embarrass Mr. Milosevic in 1995, not to hear another account from you of your great success and your great ventures in trying to embarrass him, but how would these events of 1991 being recounted in 1995 cause difficulty for him in his dealings with the West, or even with the people of Serbia? It seems to me it would do nothing but bolster his position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This story could not reinforce his position in any way. This story actually disturbed the political atmosphere in Serbia. In that year, Mr. Milosevic's party was appearing with the thesis that peace had no alternative, and they were clamoring about that. Whereas we, the Serb Radicals, felt existentially hurt by the acceptance of the Vance-Owen Plan and also the relationship between the authorities in Serbia and the authorities in Republika Srpska. There was this blockade of Republika Srpska. When I had a big rally in Loznica, when we organised a march at the Drina River, we practically used force to cross the Drina River. So the atmosphere was a very heated one. Everything I think that might be useful, I resorted to at that moment. Now, where is the problem here? Mr. Nice is just looking at very short excerpts from the campaign that we were waging then. If you would look at the entirety of all my speeches from that period of time that Mr. Nice does have, then you could have an overall picture of that campaign. If you just single out two or three sentences, that's what you see. I attacked Mr. Bogdanovic as one of the members of the leadership of the Socialist Party, bearing in mind the assumption that he took part in the taking away of our seats in parliament. In 1993, I accused him of being one of the participants of the putsch against Karadzic in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're moving away from the subject again. Just one other matter in relation to this contribution to the programme, or to the film: The impression one gets from this is that the volunteers were a group themselves. "Our volunteers proved themselves especially in the battle... when they defeated the stronger Croatian forces." And then at the foot: "But it was with those weapons that we beat the modernly equipped Croats." Now, would it be wrong to form the impression from that that this conflict occurred between forces of Serbia who were more or less exclusively your volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely wrong, Mr. Bonomy. The volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were within the Territorial Defence of Borovo Selo under the command of Vukasin Soskocanin, and it was when he asked for them that I sent my volunteers. I'm sure that the OTP has my speech from the rally in Borovo Selo in April, when I promised that we would send volunteers at the invitation of Vukasin Soskocanin. When I say "we," I identify myself with all Serb war efforts in this war, regardless of whether it's the JNA, the army of the Serb Krajina, the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, let me see whether I understand the explanation that you're giving. By saying "We were getting weapons from Milosevic's police," you were reinforcing a view that the West had of Mr. Milosevic as a person who was promoting conflict with Croatia. You were thereby reinforcing an unfavourable impression that they had of Mr. Milosevic; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I kept renewing that at the time when the West lost that impression and when they started calling Mr. Milosevic the main factor of peace in the Balkans, I actually brought up again what the West had been saying about him two years prior to that. I am taking over the arsenal in the belief that Mr. Milosevic changed his policy, and I attack him with the same arsenal that the West had attacked him with before. I'll give you another example, to make things clearer. In 1995, we, the Serb Radicals, were categorically against the Dayton accords. In Studio B and some of the other media in Serbia, we made propaganda speeches, we organised TV programmes, et cetera. Warren Christopher came, the US Secretary of State. He came to Belgrade. Mr. Milosevic complained to him about the campaign that the Serb Radical Party was waging against the Dayton agreement, through Studio B, which was considered a pro-Western TV station. Mr. Milosevic never confirmed this to me, but then, as I found out then from some other sources, Mr. Christopher said to him: "Why are you tolerating that?" After that, Nebojsa Covic, one of the key persons from the socialist regime, now an opposition person, or rather, now a member of the new regime, Nebojsa Covic annulled the privatisation of Studio B and put in an administration to be in charge of Studio B so that the Serb Radicals would totally be sealed off from the media. Why am I explaining this at such great length? It is necessary to have the historical context in mind. Everything that the regime was saying against me at the time and everything that they were accusing me of. Just as you had the opportunity of seeing today: When Mr. Nice says that I am a liar, I say that he's a liar. When one of Mr. Milosevic's top people says something like that about me, I am trying to think of the most painful thing I can think of to retaliate with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three questions, I think, before we move from this passage, and I'd like you to deal with them, if you wouldn't mind, with yes or no answers, because I think they're all susceptible to yes or no answers. Your observations here about Milosevic's police and Bogdanovic are both untrue; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. What I said in this TV programme is incorrect, and it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was within my propaganda war against Mr. Milosevic. I am not going to give you yes or no answers simply to any one of your questions, because that's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in the circumstances, I think the witness is entitled to add an explanation. What's the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next question is a very simple one, Mr. Seselj: And it was your intention at the time to say something that was untrue; yes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within the propaganda efforts of the Serb Radical Party against the authorities of Mr. Milosevic and him personally. This is the mildest kind of thing I said then. There are things that are far more vigorous than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was a lie.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. If you were an educated person, then you would have read Hannah Arendt's book, Truth and Lies in Politics. Oh, fine. So that's the best thing to do, to turn off the witness's microphone because you don't like the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bear in mind, Mr. Seselj, that this was being -- you knew this was an interview for broadcast. So when I'm sitting in front of my television, watching it, then this information, to me, coming to me, would be a lie. You might see it as propaganda within Serbia, but to someone outside of Serbia, watching television, it would be a lie.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But you who are sitting and watching television in Great Britain are used to that type of lying through your own media, because they keep lying all the time. Especially as far as the Serbs are concerned, you are snowed under with that kind of lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I, speaking for myself, find that not an appropriate way to expand upon an answer. I agree that there are certain occasions when a yes or a no may not give a complete answer, but that is an example of gratuitous abuse that you had absolutely no need to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, yesterday - you may not remember this - but I invited your explanation of your dishonest answers in the period after 1993, and you then restricted your -- you explained that you wanted to say things that weren't true about the accused Milosevic. It's now clear that you also, on your account, wanted to say things that were untrue about Bogdanovic. Who else did you want to say untrue things about in the period leading up to the giving of this interview? Who else did you wish to misrepresent? Milosevic, Bogdanovic. Who else?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody from the then regime. Sometimes I would make combinations between truthful facts and fabricated facts. Sometimes the combination was more convincing, sometimes less. But for the most part, everybody realised that I was saying that for the sake of attacking as effectively as possible, not because these were realistic facts. In the case of all -- or most of my attacks against Mr. Milosevic, the majority of Serbia was laughing. I got the aura of a brave man, a courageous man, and that contributed to the popularity of my party. Wow, he dared to say this, he dared to say that, he dared insult him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The book in which you tell us this interview is reprinted, the title of that book so that we could locate it from the number of volumes you say you've provided us? What's the title of the book in which this interview is reprinted?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You got that in one of my 80 books. I cannot remember the exact title now. But these are the books that are collections of my interviews from roughly 1995. It's not hard for you to find that. I published them in their entirety. It's about one hour's worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we're able to find this book, are we going to find in it an account by you that the interview was intentionally dishonest, in part, or not?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that book came out at the same time. And while I was in prison - I was in prison for four months under Mr. Milosevic's government - I published a book of such interviews entitled The Red Tyrant from Dedinje, The Dizdar from Dedinje, Are We in Danger of a Slobotomy? Four books altogether. Those books I published while I was in prison, and you've got all four of those books. I handed them in. So even in prison, I tried to attack him, I tried to insult him, I tried to score political points against him. So this is no exception. All my books that contain interviews from that time are similar or identical. Now, why did I publish this? I published it at the time to cause that particular effect. But later, when I published my collective works -- oh, you don't like the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move to the next clip, just then this: Is it right, as I think you confirmed yesterday, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't let a comment like that go, you see, I'm afraid. You're not being cut off from answering. You're being cut off because you're not answering. You have to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you confirm, as I think you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I continue answering now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, just answer the question which is being asked of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right, as you I think confirmed yesterday, that until the moment that you started to give evidence on behalf of this accused, you had never publicly sought to correct the record you left behind in The Death of Yugoslavia interview?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I explained that in several interviews that I gave in 1998, 1999, and in the years after that. Last night I told my legal advisors to prepare by Monday all the relevant information for me, and I hope that on Tuesday I will be able to provide you with accurate information as to when I explained all of that. Because I do not have the time to go through all this voluminous material now. But several times I explained all of that in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You explained, as you said, in 1998 and 1999 that much of what you said earlier was just bombast, was propaganda.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, then it's in the interest of the accused to have that material to put to you in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a matter of technicality, not for an observation by the witness at the moment, but for a witness to be discussing his evidence in the course of the evidence, even with his own legal advisors, is matters upon which the Court might want to consider the terms of his doing so, because of the usual injunction. May the last document be produced and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript will be 884.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now please distribute what is 25C, for the booths.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, may I say something now? It's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With no one do I discuss the content of my testimony. What I needed here was technical assistance. Every Tuesday I have conversations with the members of my expert team assisting my Defence, and I instructed them to do a technical job for me. As to what I discuss with them, it might refer to what the media are reporting, and so on and so forth. I never discuss the content of my testimony with anyone, although you never told me I shouldn't do that. However, I have heard that that's the practice and that it mustn't be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I hear the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now, then, play this part of the same recording. It's very short, and if we can deal with it on the same basis and we'll play the whole excerpt, somebody reading it in the transcript available, and seeking indications of corrections at the end. There's one particular word that the Chamber will want to possibly just be sure about in the antepenultimate line, the colour that's referred to there. We'll see what comes out of the interpreters. Again, I think the question will not be audible, but the question that can be discerned is, "When you received the weapons, was that with Milosevic's knowledge or via the police?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] That was 'all with Milosevic's knowledge.' There's no doubt of it. And as for the request, Milosevic should ask Radmilo Bogdanovic, Mihalj Kertes, General Domazetovic, for example, or somebody else, they would say --" The interpreters cannot find the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that will have to be started again and played again. And provisionally, I'm told that the colour referred to in the antepenultimate line is incorrect, but we'll have to listen to it again, if we can.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have found the reference now. "[Voiceover] That was 'all with Milosevic's knowledge.' There is no doubt. And key people from the police, with whom we had established cooperation at the time, were Radmilo Bogdanovic, Mihalj Kertes, and others. Franko Simatovic, also known as Frenki, who commanded... Therefore, from the General Staff, we mostly cooperated with General Domazetovic, who was the deputy chief of General Staff at the time, if I'm not mistaken."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a gap in the antepenultimate line. We'll come to that in a second. If, through the Chamber, I can seek the assistance of the interpreters as to whether, so far as they could discern, there were any other errors in the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters were unable to hear the colour. But apparently we believe there are no other errors -- no errors, as far as we can tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is that the interpreters just read these transcripts prepared by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what's been happening is one person has been reading it, because, of course, there's no script on the monitor, the others, I think, have been listening to it and have been asked to say whether there was any error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. They've been able to discern at the speed at which they're having to work, no errors. We have yet to deal with the question of the colour on the antepenultimate line. What we've been able to hear on this bench is not authority, and it may be that the interpreters will want to listen to it once more just to deal with the colour that's referred to. And if we could do that, I'd be grateful. We don't need, at this stage, to have it read over in English again and the interpreters can concentrate on what they hear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters heard "red berets."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, on this part of the interview, you said that receiving the weapons was all with Milosevic's knowledge, there's no doubt, and that people with whom cooperation was established included Radmilo Bogdanovic, Mihalj Kertes, and others. Was that true or was that untrue?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was untrue, with a clear political intention. The truthful part is the part that says that we cooperated with General Domazetovic, from the General Staff of the JNA. As for Borovo Selo, that weapons were found in the Territorial Defence of Borovo Selo, I was trying to accuse Radmilo Bogdanovic and Mihalj Kertes. And I insist that never in my life have I ever met Franko Simatovic. If you find a single piece of information showing that I met Franko Simatovic anywhere, then I will concede everything that you have said against my testimony. I don't even know what the man looks like in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Help us, please, then, with why you named Franko Simatovic, also known as Frenki, who commanded the Red Berets later, why did you name a man you had never met?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the unit that was formed in Golubic was called by that name. That was one unit. There was another unit formed in Serbia in 1996, and Franko Simatovic became its commander because he had a lot of war experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... unit formed in Golubic? When was it formed in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when it was formed, but it existed there in 1991. It was already there. And it existed after Captain Dragan was driven out of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive my difficulty, but you said in your last answer but one: "The unit that was formed in Golubic was called by that name, the name of the Red Berets." Do you remember I asked you not so very long ago to define the Red Berets for us and you excluded anything except the 1996 version. So what has this got to do with it? What's the Golubic Red Berets got to do with all this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are misinterpreting what I said. What you're saying is simply not true. More than once I've told you that there were various units popularly referred to as the Red Berets. Not a single one was officially called the Red Berets, not a single one, neither the one formed in Serbia in 1996 or the one formed in Serbian Krajina or the ones that existed in Republika Srpska. I insist that none of these units bore officially the name Red Berets. It was the people who called them the Red Berets because they wore red berets on their heads. However, none of them had that as an official name. Captain Dragan paraded around all the time with a red beret on his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer you actually gave at the time was, "I make a clear distinction between the Red Berets formed in 1996 and various other units who were known popularly by that name." Now, do you want to change that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Everything I've said now agrees with that, Mr. Bonomy. But the ones established in 1996 were not officially called the Red Berets either. The people referred to them as the Red Berets. Their official name was the Special Operations Unit. So there is no discrepancy between what I said previously and what I'm saying now. It's all -- it all matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was the first, if any, Red Beret unit that was a part of the state security, a special unit of the State Security Service? Which was the first one that was so formed?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to answer this question. I don't know for certain which was the first. One of the first was certainly Captain Dragan's unit. But whether it was the first or not, I couldn't swear to that. It might have been the first unit to be popularly called by that name among the people. But it was part of the Serbian army of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But let's go back to this passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not sure whether the witness understood the question. The question was as to the first Red Beret unit that was part of the state security. So your answer was that Captain Dragan's unit was the first unit which is a part of the state security. Are you saying so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not how I heard the question. I think the question was which unit apart from the one in the State Security Service was the first to bear that name. Did I understand the question correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour Judge Kwon has identified what the witness is saying as a misunderstanding, and I'm grateful. I'm happy for the Court to conclude this line of questioning, or I'll take it over, whichever the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His Honour's query is indeed a pertinent one, Mr. Seselj, and one I was trying to deal with and no doubt my shortcoming in the questioning. When, on your evidence, was the first occasion when any Red Beret unit could have come into existence as a special unit of the State Security Service? 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996? When?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, it was in 1996. That's when the JSO was established. Before 1996, there was no unit called the JSO, the Special Operations Unit. I'm certain of that. But within that unit, there were many who had previously fought in the war in various other units, including those referred to as the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when you talked about the Red Berets, what did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was in conflict with those Red Berets in the Srpska Krajina, I was in conflict with Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But when you talked about Red Berets commanded by Simatovic, who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, one should distinguish Simatovic's role in the war in the Krajina, where he turned up as a volunteer, from the role he had in 1996 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But when you were talking about the Red Berets in the interview, who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, him. You see, as far as I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "him"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Franko Simatovic, also known as Frenki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But who are these Red Berets that you were talking about him commanding in the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were the Red Berets fighting in the Krajina. Let me tell you something else: As far as I know, even volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were occasionally sent by plane to Udbina, to the Krajina, and some of them were then directed to report to the centre in Golubic. Captain Dragan publicly boasted that he had sent some of them back because they had not had a haircut, they hadn't shaved, and so on. Those are the facts. But if you want to construct something else out of those facts, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, plainly they're not facts, because you say this is inaccurate information. I mean, if they're facts, then I'm trying to be clear about them. And if, as a matter of fact, when you gave this interview, you were referring to a group known as the Red Berets, commanded by Simatovic, I would like you to tell me who that group was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you: Those were the Red Berets, active as part of the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Simatovic had a role in commanding them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For a time, he was there as a volunteer. I cannot clearly define the time, but according to what I know, he was there as a volunteer and participated in the fighting. And the experience he gained in the war there helped him get the position of commander of the JSO in 1996. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you could remind me of the date when this interview had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's March of 1995, as we are advised by the transcript provided by the television programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was before the JSO was created?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On our evidence, that is, Your Honour; evidence that the witness challenges, of course. Sorry, 1995, before it was established on his evidence. Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed you might like to answer His Honour's question, you see, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're an educated man. You heard what he said. You understand your difficulties, don't you? If something is brought into existence in 1996, omniscient though you may or may not be, you can't know what's coming in the future. So could you explain, please, to the Court how you were able to say Frenki Simatovic, who commanded the Red Berets later on? Did you have the power of foresight?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have never seen such insolence in my whole life. It says here who commanded with the Green Berets later. Who commanded the Red Berets later. I'm not saying he will do that in the future. I didn't say who will command. And in your translation here, I don't say he will command the Red Berets. Later on, he did command the Red Berets. There was no such unit at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... your volume, please. Will you now go back to the question, and we'll break it down into simple stages so that you can follow. You've given clear evidence that Simatovic controlled a unit that came into existence in 1996. The Prosecution's case, as you know, is that, on the contrary, Red Berets came into existence as a unit in 1991. Here you are speaking back to the period early 1991, and you use the phrase, "Frenki, who commanded the Red Berets -" there's a correction to the transcript - "later on." On your case, on your evidence, "later on" could only be in 1996, and you couldn't be giving this answer in 1995. Your answer does fit with the Prosecution evidence that in 1990 or the very beginning of 1991, Frenki would be somebody who would be later on commanding the Red Berets. What we want to know is: How come you were able to say something that fits with the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Nice, you have not caught me out in anything. I have caught you out. I raised my volume for a rhetorical effect, to be more impressive. Secondly, at the very beginning of the conflict, the unit popularly referred to as the Red Berets did not exist. It was formed during the conflict, when the Golubic centre for training was formed under the command of Captain Dragan. When I say "who later commanded the Red Berets," I'm not saying he's going to command from 1996 and I am predicting it. It was then that he turned up there as a volunteer and was a commander there. The fact that Frenki was in Serbian Krajina is no secret to the local people there, nor does he deny it, as far as I know. There's another problem here. You are trying to prove that this unit which Frenki commanded in the Krajina was, in establishment terms, part of the State Security Service of Serbia, and that is not true. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we're going to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've finished with this. Can we produce it, with the transcript -- and you've got a revised version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Revised transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the word "red" in already.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 885.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we turn to the next passage from the same interview, please, which for the interpreters' assistance, although they may be getting another translation - I'm not sure - is 25D. And, Your Honours, with your leave, I'll deal with one question and answer at a time, asking the booth to read the translation that's been provided and then checking after each answer whether it is accurate. And having gone through the whole of the transcript, if again this is acceptable, I'll ask my questions of the witness. If Ms. Dicklich would play the tape, please, the first question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't received the transcript in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Yes, our volunteers were in Zvornik. Arkan's volunteers participated, too, as did another formation of a certain Zuca who was under the command of the police and who is now being tried for war crimes by the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the interpreters confirm or not whether the translation appears to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We would have to hear the soundtrack again. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Play it again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question and answer, a little longer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] And how did all this come about? "Yes. We never received any orders. These were always 'requests.' Milosevic would ask us, Radmilo Bogdanovic would ask us, some general would ask us, Domazetovic for example, or somebody else. They would say: 'We need so and so many volunteers for this and that location,' and we would gather that many volunteers. When they say they need the most experienced ones, we send the most experienced ones. When they say they could also use those with not too much experience because it's nothing dangerous, then we send such people. It was always like that." That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see nodding from the booth. And then the next question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] In May 1992, I began having intensive meetings with Milosevic on a more regular basis, and back then, it was always Milosevic himself who asked for volunteers to be sent out. I mean, one did not have to convince us very much. We took this as our duty, our responsibility... except when it came to the deployment, where they were most needed... because they were known as the bravest, the most capable, and the most disciplined men." That passage is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then the last very long answer to the last question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] There were always quick agreements. For example, when Tudjman attacked Pocitelj, Divoselo and Citluk in 1993. Milosevic had some sort of agreement with him about that, but it seems Tudjman did not keep his end of the deal. They had some underhand dealings there. Milosevic was disappointed by Tudjman's actions, and therefore decided at last minute to send volunteers there. He called me and I went to him right away. He said: 'Three or four thousand volunteers need to be sent to Divoselo, Citluk and Pocitelj.' We had around 3.000 - 3.500 volunteers within two days, and Arkan brought along with him around 300 more. They were sent out from Belgrade in literally two days. There were never any problems with that. We would agree on this very quickly. This was always agreed upon in a few words. We need to go? Let's go." That seems to be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the last answer, for the purposes of the transcript, the interpreters didn't read any part of the questioning. It may be that it was inaudible at the time and I don't know if they were able to check it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not hear the beginning very well, and perhaps the year was not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question that preceded the answer that I was concerned about, Your Honours, I'll just read out what's on the printed transcript and then it can always be challenged or queried. The printed transcript of the question that led to the last answer is to the following effect. Laura Silber says: "Could you tell us about one such conversation, regarding any places where you went, or where you sent your units. How would the conversation with President Milosevic go regarding that?" And then the answer was as read out: "Those were always quick agreements..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, dealing with the four answers that are contained on this part of the transcript, asked if you or your units were in Zvornik in 1992, you answered: "Yes... Arkan's volunteers participated, too, as did a formation of Zuca who was under the command of the police and who is now being tried for war crimes." Was that answer correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The accurate part is only the first part of the answer, that our volunteers were in Zvornik and that Arkan's volunteers were in Zvornik. It is also correct that Zuca was there. The trial of Zuca had already started, and of his brother too, and I'm trying to link him up with the police and attack the regime in a forceful manner. I don't say which police, whether it was the local police or the police from Serbia. All I'm doing is launching an intrigue, a bit of intrigue, with the hope that it will lead to a political reaction and a bit of political chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he wasn't under the command of the police, under whose command was he?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, he established a paramilitary formation of a criminal nature. Now, whose command he was under, well, I assume that will come up in the trial that is being waged in Belgrade now. I wasn't there personally for me to be able to see. But what I wanted to do was to launch this intrigue, to go public with this intrigue, and to stir the water up a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did you understand the programme would be broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought it would be broadcast right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. The question was: Where did you understand the programme would be broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it was a BBC series, I thought that it would first be broadcast on the BBC network and then, through its service, be distributed who knows which television station, as was indeed what happened. So I had a very broad public before me, and I used it to target the regime. And I did that by insinuating the kind of things that I thought would be very hurtful to Mr. Milosevic and the other leaders in power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you wanted to hurt the accused, Milosevic, why didn't you say under the command of Milosevic? Because you dealt with him specifically later on. Why did you specifically put it under the command of the police?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because then it wouldn't be convincing. Even if I had concretised the police force, said specifically, it wouldn't be convincing enough. In this way, I just mentioned the police and then you don't know which police it is; this police, that police, this way, that way. So it's easier to digest and serve it out that way. If I said Mr. Milosevic in Zvornik in command of the Serb forces, well, then the journalist would say this man is mad. But since I knew how to present this kind of thing, that's what I did. I wrapped it up. And I had a political goal. I didn't have to pay attention to what Mr. Milosevic and the powers that be at the time would think about that. And I targeted him. As soon as I left prison, at the prison gates, I held similar speeches in January and I used all manner of abuse and abusive language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... understand the way you present yourself to an audience, in this case, Laura Silber, you're quick enough to be able to think, "I can change the reality just a little bit by this little lie and that will have some subsequent effect on the audience." Is that really the sort of way your mind works?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how the theory works of special warfare which in the West is systematically being developed and which I systematically learnt and studied from the well-known book by Liddel Hart, for example, The Strategy of Special Action, dating back to the '50s, and to the end of the 1970s, everything about special psychological warfare is something that I read. I have read all the books on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are other things that we can see from the video with you there in your grey suit, looking straight into the eyes of the interviewers, that you're able to tell a lie like this without any change in demeanour. You can be quite convincing, can't you, Mr. Seselj, at lies, on your own account.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'd like you to be as convincing as that when you're lying, but you're never convincing when you lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I've time and again warned you about that kind of comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll move on to the next question, with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your volunteers were in Zvornik, Arkan's volunteers are there. Under whose instruction would you have said they were there if Laura Silber had pressed you further?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would I have said then? Well, how do I know what I would have said then? Here you can see what I did in fact say. The volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party went there within the composition of the JNA, and I can guarantee that. And you cannot find a single material piece of evidence stating the contrary. They came there in JNA vehicles, JNA uniforms, and they fought there under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... at whose instruction were your volunteers sent to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does it mean under whose instructions? We received a request from the General Staff for a certain group of volunteers. We gathered up that group of volunteers, and I suppose General Domazetovic took part in that. How can I remember who it was specifically after such a long time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll go to the next question.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that they needed volunteers, I agreed to rally the volunteers and to send them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next bit, the next answer, was: "We never received orders, requests," and then you list Milosevic, Bogdanovic, and Domazetovic, as examples of those who would say we need so-and-so many volunteers for this and that location. What is this? False, true, completely false, completely true? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is once again partially true, not completely true. This is partially true, partially correct, as far as Domazetovic is concerned, and as far as Milosevic and Bogdanovic, I am putting them all there artificially, as a spanner in the works, and then they can be angry at me for having thrown them in there, into that pile, and they're impotent. They can't do anything to react properly because they tried prison and prison didn't help, just like this prison hasn't helped you to restrain me and rein me in, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have here part of your answer, which says, "When they said they needed the most experienced ones, we sent the most experienced ones, then they said we could also use those with not much experience, we'd send those people." Is that true? Were the requests different as between the experience required?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, that's how it was, because the most experienced ones were used for the most dangerous combat operations. If they were less experienced, then they might have been somewhere in the rear or some auxiliary troops, and so on. But the most experienced and the bravest went into the most serious operations. And as at the beginning we had already assumed the position that nobody who had not done their military service could go, which means they all had some sort of military training to begin with. And now it was a question of experience, how they were going to be used and deployed for certain actions, combat actions. Because some volunteers went several times, some just went once and then didn't go again. So there was fluctuation in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's just the lines or the words "Milosevic and Bogdanovic." That's just the only false bit; everything else is true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. As I say, I artificially put that in to target those two politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next question and answer: "Who, then, asked you to send your units?" and you said this: "In May 1992, I began having -" I think the word "intensive" was added - "meetings with Milosevic on a more regular basis." Just pausing there. Is that true? It is it true that you began having more intensive meetings with Milosevic in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From May 1992 to September 1993, we had more frequent meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next half of the same sentence says this: "... and back then, it was always Milosevic himself who asked for volunteers to be sent out."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, now, that's part of my intrigue. And Mr. Milosevic couldn't deny it, because there wasn't a third person at the meeting. So I did that very consciously. I launched that piece very consciously. I know that he couldn't deny it and say that he said one thing and I said another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're lying, aren't you, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it was to annoy him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the realities of what Mr. Milosevic did and you know that you've got to try to get him out of it. Very simple.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. You are lying. I did not say the truth in the interview, but here, under the solemn declaration, I am exclusively telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at the next bit of this answer: "I mean, one didn't have to convince us very much. We took this as our duty, our responsibility..." Is that correct, that you were only too happy to send your volunteers, or have them sent?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is very true. We considered it to be our duty to help the Serb people whenever they were in jeopardy, and that's what we did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with great enthusiasm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last question and answer. This is the question and answer which had Laura Silber asking you to give an account of a conversation, and you said this: "They were always quick agreements." Then you dealt with Tudjman's attack on Pocitelj and Divoselo and Citluk in 1993. You said: "Milosevic had some sort of agreements with him about that, it seems Tudjman didn't keep his end of the deal... underhand dealings. Milosevic was disappointed by Tudjman's actions and ... decided at the last minute to send volunteers there. He called me and I went to him right away." Let's just pause there, shall we? Did you, in 1993, have a meeting with Milosevic about the deployment of volunteers to deal with the attack at Pocitelj, Divoselo or Citluk?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Categorically, I say no. With respect to the attack on Pocitelj, Divoselo and Citluk, we had an agreement with the representatives of Republika Srpska Krajina in Belgrade, and those representatives, or the representative offices organised buses and it was in those buses that we sent out the volunteers. However, Tudjman's attack on Pocitelj, Divoselo, and Citluk at the time stopped, the volunteers were there for a few days. As the fighting ceased, they returned without having joined in the combat. And that happened in 1993. And you can check that out very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's read the whole thing, the last part of this, but without any reference to the name "Milosevic," and see whether the rest of it is true. "[Someone] called me and I went to him right away. He said: 'Three or four thousand volunteers need to be sent to Divoselo, Pocitelj, Citluk.' We had around 3.000 - 3.500 volunteers within two days, and Arkan brought along with him around 300. They were sent out from Belgrade in literally two days. There were never any problems with that. We would agree on this very quickly. This was already agreed upon in a few words. We need to go? Let's go." Now, as I've read it, substituting on one occasion the word "he" for "Milosevic," would it be completely accurate?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody called. Somebody came to the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party from the represented offices of Srpska Krajina in Okreska Street [phoen]. I can't remember who it was, somebody from their representation there. They came to our war staff. I was informed that that was necessary, I agreed, and the volunteers were rallied and sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you have got a famously good memory, as you've told us. Just think back, please. Who was it who came to your office and asked for these three or four thousand volunteers?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't come to my office. He came to the war headquarters or staff and he was a functionary of the representative offices of Srpska Krajina in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your political party had a department called the war staff, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... interest, it's a bit of a digression, but in light of an earlier question from the Bench, why should a political party have a war staff?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was a great national need for that political party to rally volunteers and send them to the JNA, for the war, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... or just the war staff, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the other institutions of the party were peacetime ones, and the war staff dealt with rallying volunteers and sending them to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... send volunteers to do peaceful things in countries, Mr. Seselj, not in countries in the other part of the former Yugoslavia, did you, or did you just send people to engage in fighting?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent them to engage in fighting and realise the tasks and goals of the JNA. So don't attach any peaceful policy to me. I was never an advocate of peace at every price, at all costs. I'm an adversary to that now. I don't accept a pact with the Americans, and what the Americans are doing today in the Balkans are only creating conditions for a new war. No, I've just said that for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who came to your office and asked you to do this? You deployed three to four thousand volunteers. Who asked you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't remember after so much time all the names. Somebody did come, a high-ranking official of the representative offices of Srpska Krajina from Belgrade. They had their headquarters in Terazija Square, the centre, the very heart of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you understand the significance of these questions, Mr. Seselj? You see, if you give me a name, I can go and find out from that person what he, or it may even be a she, would say. If you don't give me a name, it's rather like your previous answer about two people in a room; one can never deny the other. We can never prove it, you see. Can you give us a name so that we can go and check?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you expect me to remember the name of the person who worked in the representative offices of Srpska Krajina in 1993 in Belgrade? Go on. Tell me that. How can I be expected to do that? In these two and a half years that I've been in prison, I've forgotten many of the names of the people I knew. I can't remember a single telephone number any more. Now you want me to remember the name of the man who came from the representative offices of Srpska Krajina. I can't remember the name of a single army officer, high-ranking army officer who came to our party headquarters, and many colonels came, captains of frigates, et cetera. Why would I have to remember them, their names? Only stupid people remember numbers and names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, these answers you gave reveal the truth about the accused's active, knowing, and criminal involvement in the sending of volunteers to fight in other parts of the former Yugoslavia, and you know that to be true.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. First of all, the sending of volunteers was absolutely not criminal; it was patriotic. And secondly, in sending volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, Slobodan Milosevic never took part in that. He never had any part in sending that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could the tape please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 886.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we now turn to -- can we now look at the next passage, which is 25E, for the interpreters. A fresh translation is being distributed. And I think with the length of the first answer, if we can break it into perhaps two segments and have the comments of the -- not the comments, the help of the interpretation booth, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] In May 1992, Milosevic took definitely the whole control over the JNA. That's when the new constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was proclaimed, and that's when he really and formally and literally became the most important man in the country. The man who makes all the decisions. ... And the Zvornik operation..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to those first couple of sentences --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Everything appears to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move on, there was nothing read out from the question because there was nothing audible over the machinery here in court. But it will help the witness to know that the question in the transcript, from those who have been able to listen, I think, with magnified sound, was: "How did things proceed when you headed towards Zvornik? Who told you to go there? How did that work?" And then we have the first part of the answer. If we can pick it up from there, please

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Everything was planned in Belgrade. Bosnian Serb forces took part in it, and they comprised a greater part of it. Meanwhile, the special units, and the best-equipped units came from this side, they were direct police units, the so-called Red Berets, special units of the Security Service of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Pausing there, those four lines, any comment from the interpretation booth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Everything appears more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The way it appears in the translation, and maybe you won't be able to remember this - I ask the question through the Court, of course - is that it starts off with the sentence: "And the Zvornik operation was planned in Belgrade," with the word "Zvornik" included. I don't know if you can remember, through the Court, whether the word "Zvornik" was actually used.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, in the first playing of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Let's move on to the next section.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] There were volunteers from the SRS, Arkan's volunteers, and another smaller group of volunteers under the control of the police. The army engaged little in that operation, it mainly gave artillery support where it was needed. The operation was well thought out over a long period of time, so nothing was done in haste or anxiety with last-minute urgent requests for this or that. It was all well organised and well carried out, until... once the looting started then nobody could control it any more."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to the accuracy of that passage?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Until the end of hostilities." It says was, "well carried out until..." and the three dots were "the end of hostilities, once the looting started..." That's just a phrase that was left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question, then, please, if we can play the next question and answer in one. Whether the question comes out or not, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Who devised this and how was it carried out? "This was devised by key people of the SDB, among whom was Franko Simatovic, Frenki, and he was one of the main executors. There were others whose names I haven't even memorised. Our volunteers gathered and their central meeting point was in Loznica from where they headed to Zvornik. Duke Cvetinovic was in charge of them, and he directly received orders from the Commanders of the Special Forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Accuracy of that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Special Units." Otherwise it is more or less accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Special units" comes in where?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "... from the Commanders of the Special Units," and we heard "commanders," in the plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, "Duke," is of course the translation for Vojvoda Cvetinovic. Let's just deal with the answers that you gave, starting at the bottom and working back up. Is it right that Vojvoda Cvetinovic was in charge in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he was one of the volunteers there, and he did command a certain number of men, I don't know how large. But he was prominent in the fighting. Secondly, all those volunteers were within the composition of the JNA and I here am ascribing this to the security service, targeting it, because that service on the opposite side -- on the other side was trying to destroy the Serbian Radical Party. You have heard about Ljubisa Petkovic, my vice-president, who was chief of the war staff. At the end of 1993, the state security system wanted to recruit him and to break up -- as a Trojan horse, to break up the Radical Party. Those were the methods used by that service against us. So I am attacking the service for anything I can think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So where you said that he directly received orders from the commander of the special units, what should you have said, to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was from the JNA command in charge that he received orders. Who it was exactly is not hard to establish. Do you really think that so many names can be memorised? Secondly, I wasn't there, so it wasn't for me to remember all those names. I just know that volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were disciplined there and -- that they were highly disciplined, and as soon as the Zvornik operation was over, they returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The previous sentence says: "Our volunteers gathered at their central meeting point, which was Loznica, from where they headed to Zvornik." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gathered together in Belgrade, and they went to Zvornik from there. Before Zvornik, they stopped in Loznica. Cvetinovic is from Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Previous sentence gives this answer: "This was devised by key people from the SDB..." True?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I'm trying to impute this to the key people of the SDB, attacking the State Security Service, because I'm actually returning the blow. I'm categorically stating that the reservists --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The volunteers went to the JNA, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
