utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that is part of their service booklets. But this is the time when I was waging a campaign against the SDB, and that was a question of survival for us in the Serb Radical Party. Because the security service used different perfidious methods to cause discord among us. They tried to recruit people and stir trouble in our ranks. We were clashing so violently with the SDB then that they really did not choose their methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me how this would upset the SDB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would politically compromise them. That was the time of peace initiatives. It was 1995. It could compromise the authorities of Slobodan Milosevic, and so on. That was the time of not shying away from anything in our mutual conflicts. Mr. Milosevic himself did not appear, but his authorities spared no effort to attack us. Mr. Nice is not really up to date. In addition to this TV programme, he could have found at least 100 similar TV interviews of mine within that campaign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've got this one. Can you remember if you were able to come up with anything more recent than 1991 to upset them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what could that have been? This wasn't in 1991, sir. This was in 1992. I was saying other things as well. I was waging a campaign in various fields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In 1992, did you come up with anything more recent that might upset them in the course of this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but that had to do with domestic policy. In 1995, there weren't war conflicts of this kind. After all, there was a considerable lull in the fighting then. This was before the Croatian Operation Storm and Flash. April and May was a period of a lull in the fighting, when the battle for Bihac ended, late in 1994, beginning of 1995. Then there was a lull in the fighting on all fronts. But in the economics sphere, I launched similar attacks, and also in the field of domestic policies and so on. So there is an abundance of interviews of mine in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You understand, don't you, that if somebody says things that are different from one occasion to another, it may be a sign that he's a liar. And you've told us you're telling us the truth here. So let's just focus on that, shall we? You say, in respect of pinning this on the SDB -- I think it's just gone off the screen. Only five minutes ago, I think, when I suggested to you that you were covering up for the accused because what he was doing was criminal in sending volunteers to fight in the other parts of the former Yugoslavia, you said: "It's not true. Sending of volunteers was absolutely not criminal. It was patriotic." Let's go back to see what you said about the same period of time precisely and why this would compromise the SDB because you may like to consider your position and tell us which is the truth. You say -- you're attacking -- by putting this false account in, you're attacking the State Security Service, waging a compromise against them. And then His Honour Judge Bonomy said: "How would this upset them?" And you said: "It would politically compromise them." Explain, but preferably in a quiet voice so that we can follow it, the contrast between your two answers: It would have been lawful for the accused to do it, but that by lying about it and saying the SDB did it, you're compromising them on a patriotic duty. Go on, tell us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Then I was trying to spoil the peaceful policy of Slobodan Milosevic, by resorting to all means. At that time, in the spring, I had 20 rallies all over the Serb Krajina, attacking, attacking, attacking, attacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't have forever. The question is actually quite a simple one. You said you lied about the SDB because it would compromise them. You said the same action would have been legal if it had been done by Milosevic, because it was lawful at the time to send volunteers. Now, which is it, please?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, that's not true. You are making up a false construction here. First of all, it is patriotic duty to help the Western Serbs. But since international recognition followed, that is to say, both of Croatia and of Bosnia-Herzegovina, institutionally Serbia could not interfere. But here, in this interview, when I was clashing with Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, I'm claiming that they were interfering institutionally, and in that way, I'm compromising him and his government. For any normal person, this would be very clear. And I'm speaking in a normal tone of voice. And for me, this is a normal tone of voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, I'm just going to deal with that very briefly. You've been shouting at this Court for several days and you've been maintaining the fiction that you can't speak quietly. It is a fiction. You can speak perfectly quietly if you wish to. And you gave the game away in your very last answer before the last break when you explained that you'd raised your tone for rhetorical purposes. The truth is, you've been shouting at this Court in an endeavour to add rhetorical force to the assertions you're making; true? You're quite capable of speaking quietly if you want to.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have perfect self-control, and I can control everything I do, physically and verbally. Secondly, I speak normally. I do not shout. I speak loud and clear and precisely. Now, you are envious because of the depth of my voice and because of the quality of my voice. You have to ask for hormonal therapy in order to improve upon your own voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must say, we were expecting you to make a sort of cheap personal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remark at some stage and we're really pleased that you've done it, and thank you for meeting everybody's expectations. But tell us this: Did you shout at Laura Silber? Because we've seen a lot of tape. Has there been some change in your self-control or have you got hard of hearing or has your voice-box changed? Just tell us. Have your hormones changed? What is it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you are dying of laughter at my cheap tricks. Now, what would happen if I resorted to more expensive, dear tricks? You might burst of laughter. Laura Silber seemed like a youngish woman to me, quite good-looking, even with feminine curves, and I adjusted my voice to that. If I were talking to these ladies here, I would adjust my voice to that. I'm talking to you as to a haughty Prosecutor, and I'm trying to show that you are not all that smart. I'm not saying you're stupid. You're just not all that smart. I'm speaking in a particular way because I'm in a courtroom. I speak in a different way when I'm visited by people in my office, and I speak yet in another way --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the first eight days, you weren't speaking to me at all, you were speaking in what you've been telling us was an endeavour to tell the whole truth to the three Judges, and you shouted at them for rhetorical purposes. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the first answer to this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are not right. I did not shout at them. I spoke as one does in a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's get on with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the middle of the answer, there's this interesting passage. Having said that Milosevic took control of the JNA completely, you said that the Zvornik operation was planned in Belgrade. Bosnian forces took part and comprised a greater part of it. "Meanwhile, the special units and the best equipped units came from this side, and they were police units -" and then this - "the so-called Red Berets, special units of the Security Service of Serbia." Now, it's the same point that was raised in the last tape, or the last tape but one, indeed by a question initially from His Honour Judge Kwon. On your account, Mr. Seselj, how could you, in March 1995, have been speaking of Red Berets, special units of the security service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I construed that on the basis of the fact that Frenki was a volunteer in the Krajina. As a matter of fact, in the government of the Serb Krajina, he was in charge of security and intelligence affairs or something like that. I don't know exactly what the official name of his position was. I was speculating, because a large number of people had been earlier on among the volunteers in the Serb Krajina, and I was again creating an intrigue, and again I expected it to be a political bombshell and to go off. And the Red Berets from the Krajina were something that people had heard of by then. So I was using Frenki's name to link this up to the State Security Service of Serbia. I construed that. And quite successfully, at that, because even you swallowed it and you based your indictment against Mr. Milosevic on that, and look what's happened now; it's gone down the drain. And you have my statement that was given for political reasons. It was preconceived. It was calculated to cause political damage. But you haven't got a shred of material evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that answer, then we'll look at something different. You make it clear that the Red Berets to whom you're referring in this part of your answer was indeed Frenki. So we can exclude all consideration of Dragan and his men. This is Frenki. Yes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm just reading your answer.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, you're not reading it well. First of all, I don't know whether Frenki was in Zvornik at all. I doubt it. I think he wasn't. I'm just construing things. I'm putting him in a particular context, knowing that Frenki is a nervous man, that that would really irritate him. So I am trying to provoke him, rile him. I know that Frenki was in Krajina, and that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first meet Frenki?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met Frenki here, in Scheveningen, in prison, when he was here -- when he arrived in the summer of 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you know he's a nervous man?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard stories about him. He was considered to be a man with a very short temper, nervous and so on and so forth. Those are the kind of stories I heard about him. It's not that Frenki is an unknown person altogether. But I don't know him, and you haven't got a shred of evidence to the effect that I had met him anywhere. Even if he wanted to prove something like that, he'd be powerless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I may have missed this, I probably have, but what was it you had against Frenki at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I had against Frenki was the fact that he was a high official of the State Security Service. He was one of the best-known associates of Jovica Stanisic in the public, and I was targeting the service because they were doing their best to destroy the Serb Radical Party. That was a clash between their service and a political party. If I were to tell you about all of that, everything that the service fabricated against me and said in public about me, it would take up a lot of time, starting with them saying that I was a Croat. And to tell you the truth, that afflicted me the most. You know, when they said that I was a Croat, the State Security Service used an opposition party, Vuk Draskovic, the Serbian Renewal Movement, through Milan Komnenic, Aleksandar Taskovic and other agents in their ranks. And I could tell you about that all day, everything that the service did against me, in order to understand the context when I lash out at the service. But my books are full of that, when I write about everything that the service did against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The only other questions on this answer, I just have it in mind, is this: That therefore, on your account, when you were talking to Laura Silber in March 1995, you were able, but entirely by coincidence, to say -- to speak of a Red Beret unit connected to Frenki - because you acknowledge that it's connected to Frenki - of the security service of Serbia, it was entirely a matter of coincidence that you were able to say that when such a unit came into existence in 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you have to take a look at my other interviews from that time and you will see that this is no exception. Secondly, the fact that Frenki was a high official of the State Security Service and that he was a volunteer in the Serb Krajina and that at that time he had that unit there. I don't know exactly what his position was in it. He had that unit of the Red Berets. It's enough for me to link all of that up together. Look at what you've linked up here without a shred of material evidence. But I stand by the fact that the Special Operations Unit was founded in 1996 and that this unit of the Red Berets from Krajina had no institutional links to the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last question on this answer is this: A couple of sentences, or one sentence later on, you speak of the operation in Zvornik and in Belgrade, and you say: "The army engaged little in that operation, it mainly gave artillery support where it was needed." True?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was engaged. They also gave artillery support. It was the fort above Zvornik that the army targeted with the artillery. And that the army was engaged little, well, the army was the one that was in charge of all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this answer, I'm just going to finish with this, for this question. On this answer -- we know what you say is untrue, but on this answer, Milosevic, the army, the police, Frenki Simatovic, the Red Berets, and indeed Arkan, and your volunteers, all involved together in the attack on Zvornik. That's the account you gave to Laura Silber. I'm going to suggest to you that it was true.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am asserting that that is not correct. I claim that the JNA was carrying out operations in Zvornik, that the forces of Republika Srpska were taking part in these operations, and they had just been established. Also, the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party took part, as well as Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May this be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 887.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, as for Mr. Simatovic, do you know from when he engaged himself in security service work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I think that he was there for a long time as a professional and that he worked his way up from the lowest ranks of agents all the way up. But I don't know exactly how long this took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So was he involved in security work before he went to Zvornik as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said that he went to Zvornik as a volunteer. He went to Republika Srpska Krajina as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's my mistake. Except for that, could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not give you an exact, reliable answer to that now. I know that he did work for the State Security Service and then went to the volunteers. But we had an even higher-ranking person from the police; Radovan Stojicic, Badza. Later on he was a colonel-general in the police. He went as a volunteer to the eastern part. I think that Frenki's case was fairly similar to that, but I don't have any reliable knowledge to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to play you a short extract from an exhibit. We've just produced for the assistance of the Court English translations of the relevant part. The document is a video taken of a ceremony, Exhibit 390.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're giving me everything in the English language. That is wrong altogether, and I don't know English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you'll hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... aside, Mr. Seselj, and listen to what's going to come over the loudspeakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, do you have a picture yet on your screen of Frenki Simatovic? Do you see him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now would you listen to what he says and we'll follow it in our transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. President, we thank you for accepting the invitation to attend the ceremony marking the anniversary of the formation of the Special Operations Unit of the State Security Service. It was constituted on the 4th of May, 1991, at the time of the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and since it emerged has constantly worked to protect national security in circumstances where the existence of the Serbian people was directly jeopardised throughout its entire ethnic area. Its combat operations were anti-terrorist, directed at preventing war crimes, mass retaliation and genocide. "From the first moment of its existence..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you seen this video before yourself, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it when you played it during Mr. Milosevic's trial. I think that I was still in Belgrade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know that this video shows the accused, Milosevic, reviewing the Red Berets, and it shows, although we can easily find it for you if you want it to be confirmed, shows him standing in the room while this speech is being addressed to him by Frenki Simatovic? So he speaks of formation in May of 1991; true or false.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franko Simatovic, Frenki, speaks of that, but his speech is not clear, what he means by it. He continues his warrior tradition in a unit that was institutionally established in Serbia in 1996 as the JSO. In the Krajina, it did not exist as the JSO and as a State Security Service unit of Serbia. In Krajina, Franko Simatovic was in charge of security and intelligence affairs on the Republic of Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't want to take too much time, but just to remind the Court and to remind you, since you've seen it, and we have - those of us reading the English, but you must take it from me - we have the English translation of the first part in front of us. He speaks of the enormous contribution of the unit, the 47 killed, the 250 wounded at 50 locations. He gives the history of the unit, of its formation, of its engagement in battles from October 1991 with Croatian forces in Benkovac, Stari Gospic, Plitvice, Glina, Kostajnica and others, and so on. This is the Red Berets, under Simatovic, a special unit that you describe in your interviews, and this shows that what you were saying to Laura Silber, far from being false, was absolutely correct insofar as it referred to the Red Berets, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. In order to explain this more easily, I'm going to compare this to something that happened within the Serb Radical Party. With some political friends of mine, in January 1990, I established the Serbian Freedom-loving Movement, and we united with Vuk Draskovic into the Serbian Renewal Movement and we removed Draskovic and he set up the same party, or rather, a similar party under the same name. And then we changed our name into the Serb Chetnik Movement. In then February 1993 we united with the National Radical Party into the Serb Radical Party. I keep invoking my previous party efforts from 1990, and I made this part of our statute. Formally, it was in March 1992 that the Serb Radical Party was registered and we celebrate our jubilee over a year before that. So people who had already taken part in the war, and probably the majority of the members of this unit were in that unit in the Krajina, they're simply building on that tradition. But how can that be explained to Arkan's people, who are also included in 1996? How can you explain the rest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at the video as a whole, it's clear that he's describing a unit of single identity, setting out its history and ultimately people are rewarded, people who died years before are referred to, and so on. And the accused Milosevic is standing there, honouring this group of people. Was he taking part in a sham, do you say?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why wouldn't Mr. Milosevic pay tribute to all the Serbs who died in the war, honour them? They are members of our nation. But I'm saying there was no institutional link. And I'm referring to the traditions of Vojin Popovic and Tankosic, the Chetnik vojvodas, before World War I, Vasilije Trbojevic and some others, and then the traditions of Drazen Mihajlovic as well. But I cannot say, ah, now, there's an institutional link between us here now. We Serbs are a united people and a position presented this way by Frenki Simatovic, Frenki, emerges from the fact that we are a united nation. But institutional links between those units, the Red Beret units in Srpska Krajina and the State Security Service of Serbia, never existed, to the best of my knowledge. Now, the fact that the State Security Service, once the war was already over, took over most of these members and took over many of Arkan's men and took over many fighters from Serbian Krajina who fled, is something quite different. But to divide us Serbs and to say that we're not one people, one nation, and look at it that way, that's impossible. There was no institutional link, and I insist upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It shows quite clearly that creation in 1991 of a unit that was then partly transferred in September 1991 to Serbia, as we can see, and took over a building in 1995, which was named after Radoslav Kostic, who died years earlier, this shows the creation in May 1991, by this accused, who honoured it, of an organisation that, on your own evidence, because you'll remember telling me this, could never have been justified lawfully, and that's why you're lying about it, Mr. Seselj, isn't it? You know you've all been caught.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- no. No. You didn't catch me out lying. I'm catching you out all day today lying, and I did so yesterday too, Mr. Nice. You're the only person lying here. And I testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you know very well what I'm going to speak to you about. It's a common practice in courts for counsel for one side to put to a witness for the other side that he's not telling the truth. That's his professional duty. It's not a personal matter. He does so on the basis of the evidence and instructions that he has. It is not proper for you to respond in the way that you have done, and I've explained that to you time and again. We will adjourn now and resume on Wednesday of next week at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of September, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
